questions.question: What is Inversion of Control (IoC) and Dependency Injection (DI) in Spring?
questions.title: Inversion of Control (IoC) and Dependency Injection in Spring
questions.direct_answer: IoC is the design principle where the framework — not your code — controls object creation and lifecycle. Dependency Injection is the mechanism Spring uses to implement IoC: dependencies are provided to a class from the outside rather than created internally. This decoupling is what makes Spring applications testable, configurable, and loosely coupled.

interviewer_intent.testing: Whether the candidate distinguishes the principle (IoC) from the mechanism (DI) and can articulate why this matters beyond textbook definitions.
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Treating IoC and DI as synonyms — IoC is the broad principle (framework calls you, not you calling the framework), DI is one specific way to achieve it.
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Explain why constructor injection is preferred over field injection: it makes dependencies explicit, enforces immutability, and allows unit testing without a Spring context.

sections.title: The `new` Keyword Is a Hard Dependency — and IoC Is Spring's Answer
sections.content:
Every Java tutorial shows the same starting point: a service class that creates its dependencies with `new`. `OrderService` doing `new StripeGateway()` inside its constructor couples the two classes permanently — swap payment providers, write a unit test, or deploy to staging and you're editing `OrderService` every time. The `new` keyword isn't just syntax; it's a hard dependency on a specific implementation.

**Inversion of Control** (IoC) is Spring's answer to this. Instead of your class reaching out to create its dependencies, the framework controls object creation and lifecycle. Your class declares what it needs — Spring decides how, when, and with which implementation to provide it. This is the Hollywood Principle: "Don't call us, we'll call you." Spring's `ApplicationContext` is the IoC container: it reads your `@Component`, `@Service`, and `@Bean` declarations, instantiates beans, resolves their dependencies, and manages the full lifecycle from creation to destruction.

**Dependency Injection** (DI) is the specific mechanism Spring uses to implement IoC. Instead of `OrderService` calling `new StripeGateway()`, Spring injects a `PaymentGateway` implementation through the constructor. The class depends on an interface, not a concrete type. Spring provides `StripeGateway` in production, `SandboxGateway` in staging, and a mock in tests — and `OrderService` never changes.

The distinction interviewers probe: **IoC is the principle, DI is one mechanism to achieve it.** Service Locator is another IoC mechanism — the class asks a registry for dependencies. DI inverts even that: the container pushes dependencies in without the class asking. Spring uses DI. Knowing this difference — and explaining the `new` keyword cost with a concrete example — is what separates a textbook answer from a production-aware one.

sections.title: The `new` Keyword Trap: One Coupling, Four Problems
Constructor Injection: Declare the Need, Let Spring Fulfill It
Constructor vs Setter vs Field Injection: The Differences That Matter
sections.content:
The three injection styles look like alternatives. They're not equally valid for mandatory dependencies. The rows that matter most: `final` fields (immutability), unit testability without Spring, and how circular dependencies are surfaced.

| | Constructor | Setter | Field |
|---|---|---|---|
| `final` fields | Yes | No | No |
| Unit testable without Spring | Yes — `new Foo(dep)` | Yes — `foo.setDep(dep)` | No — reflection required |
| Dependencies visible | Yes — constructor signature | Yes — setter method | No — hidden `@Autowired` |
| For mandatory deps | Yes | No | Either |
| For optional deps | No | Yes | Either |
| Circular dep detection | Startup — `BeanCurrentlyInCreationException` | Runtime | Runtime |
| `@Autowired` required | No (single ctor, Spring 4.3+) | Yes | Yes |
| Spring team stance | Preferred | Optional deps only | Discouraged |

The circular dependency row is the most interview-relevant. Constructor injection surfaces the design problem at startup — fail fast, fix early. Field injection hides it until runtime through partially-initialized proxies.

sections.title: Three Things Constructor Injection Gets Right That the Others Don't
When Spring Injects — and Why @Autowired Fields Are Null in the Constructor
sections.content:
Spring resolves dependencies at different points depending on the injection style, and the timing difference causes the most common Spring debugging session for developers mixing injection styles.

**Constructor injection** resolves dependencies before the object exists. Spring builds the full dependency graph, determines instantiation order, and passes all required beans as constructor arguments. The object is fully wired from the first line of the constructor body — no partially-initialized state is possible.

**Field and setter injection** happen after the object is created. The bean is instantiated first (no-arg constructor), then `AutowiredAnnotationBeanPostProcessor` runs in the `postProcessProperties` phase, using `Field.setAccessible(true)` to write into private fields. This is why an `@Autowired` field read inside the constructor returns `null` — the post-processor hasn't run yet. Move that initialization logic to `@PostConstruct`.

This timing difference explains the circular dependency behavior interviewers probe. With constructor injection, Spring must resolve A before creating B and B before creating A — an impossibility caught at startup with `BeanCurrentlyInCreationException`. With field injection, Spring creates A (uninitialized), creates B, injects A into B, then finishes A — hiding the cycle through partially-initialized beans.

For optional dependencies, avoid `@Autowired(required = false)` — it silently injects `null` and propagates NPE risk to every call site. The better approach: `private final Optional<MetricsService> metricsService` — Spring wraps the result, optionality is explicit in the type, and there's no NPE risk.

sections.title: Key Points
sections.content:
- **IoC ≠ DI** — IoC is the principle (framework controls lifecycle, not your class); DI is one mechanism. Service Locator is another — in DI, the container pushes dependencies in without the class asking.
- **Spring 4.3+: no `@Autowired` on single-constructor classes** — Spring uses the sole constructor automatically. Add `@RequiredArgsConstructor` (Lombok) + `private final` fields for zero-boilerplate constructor injection.
- **Constructor injection = startup failure for circular deps** — `BeanCurrentlyInCreationException` at boot. Field/setter injection hides circular deps until runtime via partially-initialized proxy beans.
- **`@Autowired` fields are `null` in the constructor body** — `AutowiredAnnotationBeanPostProcessor` fires after construction, not during. Reading field-injected deps in the constructor causes NPE; move logic to `@PostConstruct`.
- **`Optional<T>` over `@Autowired(required = false)`** — `Optional<MetricsService>` makes optionality explicit in the type; `required = false` silently injects `null` and propagates NPE risk to every call site.
- **`final` = JVM-guaranteed immutability** — constructor-injected `final` fields are set once, safe across threads. Field injection cannot use `final`. Immutable beans eliminate a class of threading bugs common in shared singleton state.

sections.title: How to Answer This Verbally
sections.content:
Spring's whole model is built around one insight — the `new` keyword is a hard dependency. When `OrderService` does `new StripeGateway()` inside its constructor, those two classes are permanently coupled. You can't swap the gateway, test in isolation, or configure differently per environment without modifying `OrderService`. IoC and Dependency Injection are Spring's solution to that problem.

**Inversion of Control**
- IoC means the framework controls object creation and lifecycle — your class doesn't reach out and wire itself
- Spring's `ApplicationContext` is the IoC container: it reads your `@Component` and `@Bean` declarations, creates beans, resolves dependencies, and manages their lifecycle
- The shift: you declare what you need, Spring decides which implementation to provide based on what's registered

**Dependency Injection**
- DI is the specific mechanism — dependencies come in from outside the class (constructor, setter, or field) instead of being created internally with `new`
- This is what makes testing clean: `new OrderService(mockGateway)` in a unit test, `StripeGateway` in production — `OrderService` never changes
- IoC and DI are not synonyms: IoC is the principle, DI is one mechanism. Service Locator is another IoC pattern — in DI, the container pushes dependencies in; the class doesn't ask for them

**Constructor injection**
- The Spring team's recommendation for mandatory dependencies: `final` fields, explicit constructor signature, testable without the container
- Since Spring 4.3, a class with one constructor doesn't need `@Autowired` — Spring uses it automatically. Add Lombok's `@RequiredArgsConstructor` and you get zero-boilerplate injection
- The practical tell: constructor injection exposes circular dependencies at startup (`BeanCurrentlyInCreationException`). Field injection hides them and produces partially-initialized proxy beans that fail only at runtime

Field injection looks cleaner — one `@Autowired` per field — but you can't unit test without Spring, dependencies are invisible, and `final` is impossible. In modern Spring projects, constructor injection for mandatory deps and setter injection for optional ones is the standard. Field injection is a legacy pattern worth moving away from.

questions.question: What are the differences between constructor injection, field injection, and setter injection?
questions.title: Constructor Injection vs Field Injection vs Setter Injection
questions.direct_answer: Constructor injection wires dependencies through the constructor, making them final and available immediately — it is the Spring team's recommended approach. Field injection uses @Autowired on fields directly (convenient but not testable without a container). Setter injection uses @Autowired on setter methods, allowing optional or re-injectable dependencies.

sections.title: Why the Spring Team Picked a Winner — and Most Codebases Still Get It Wrong
sections.content:
The three injection styles aren't equally valid alternatives — they represent a **spectrum from explicit to hidden dependency management**, and the choice has consequences for testability, immutability, and how fast design problems surface.

**Constructor injection** wires dependencies at object creation time. The constructor parameter list is the class's contract — every collaborator is visible, fields can be `final`, and you can test with plain `new` and mocks. No Spring context, no reflection. This is why the Spring team officially recommends it for all mandatory dependencies.

**Field injection** uses `@Autowired` directly on private fields. It looks clean — no constructor boilerplate — but the simplicity is deceptive. Dependencies are invisible from outside the class, `final` is impossible, and testing requires either `ReflectionTestUtils` or a full Spring context. Worse, it hides design problems: a class with 12 field-injected dependencies looks tidy while violating Single Responsibility.

**Setter injection** lives in the middle. Dependencies are visible via method signatures and settable in tests, but they can't be `final` and require null-checks since they might not be called. The legitimate use case is optional dependencies — collaborators that enhance behavior but aren't required for the class to function.

sections.title: The Lombok Shortcut and Why Kotlin Gets Constructor Injection for Free
sections.content:
In practice, most Spring teams use **Lombok's `@RequiredArgsConstructor`** to eliminate constructor boilerplate while keeping `final` fields. The annotation generates a constructor for every `final` field, giving you the benefits of constructor injection without writing the constructor yourself.

This works because Spring 4.3+ automatically uses the **sole constructor** of a class for injection — no `@Autowired` annotation needed. A class with `@RequiredArgsConstructor` and three `final` fields gets a three-argument constructor that Spring discovers and invokes automatically.

Kotlin takes this further. Spring treats Kotlin **primary constructors** identically to Java constructor injection. A Kotlin class `class OrderService(private val gateway: PaymentGateway)` is constructor-injected without any annotations at all. The `val` keyword makes the field `final` by default, and the primary constructor is the only constructor, so Spring resolves it automatically. This is why the testability story is identical across JVM languages — constructor injection is a design pattern, not a Java-specific trick.

questions.question: How does @Autowired work internally? What role does BeanPostProcessor and reflection play?
questions.title: How @Autowired Works Internally
questions.direct_answer: @Autowired is processed by AutowiredAnnotationBeanPostProcessor, which uses Java reflection to scan each bean's fields, setters, and constructors for the annotation. It then queries the BeanFactory to resolve matching beans by type — and by name if there is ambiguity — before injecting them via reflection.

sections.title: Why @Autowired Isn't Magic — It's a BeanPostProcessor Running Reflection
sections.content:
Most developers treat `@Autowired` as compiler magic — annotate a field, and Spring somehow fills it in. The reality is a **concrete processing pipeline** that runs after the object is constructed, and understanding it explains why field-injected dependencies are `null` inside the constructor and why constructor injection behaves fundamentally differently.

The key player is `AutowiredAnnotationBeanPostProcessor`, a `BeanPostProcessor` that Spring registers automatically when you use `@SpringBootApplication` or `<context:annotation-config/>`. It scans every bean class for `@Autowired`, `@Value`, and JSR-330's `@Inject` annotations, builds a list of injection points, and resolves each one from the `BeanFactory`.

The timing distinction matters. **Constructor injection** resolves dependencies before the object exists — Spring looks up the required beans, then passes them as constructor arguments. The object is fully wired from the first line of the constructor body. **Field and setter injection** happen after construction — the `BeanPostProcessor` fires during the `postProcessProperties` phase, using `Field.setAccessible(true)` to bypass `private` modifiers and write directly into the field. This is why an `@Autowired` field is `null` if you read it inside the constructor — the post-processor hasn't run yet.

sections.title: How Spring Finds Injection Points Before Any Bean Exists
sections.content:
Before Spring creates any bean instance, it parses every `@Component`-annotated class into a `BeanDefinition` — a metadata object that describes the class name, scope, constructor arguments, and dependencies. During this phase, `AutowiredAnnotationBeanPostProcessor` inspects the class for injection metadata.

The processor scans three locations: **constructors** annotated with `@Autowired` (or the sole constructor in Spring 4.3+), **fields** with `@Autowired` or `@Value`, and **methods** with `@Autowired`. For each discovered injection point, it creates an `InjectionMetadata` object that caches the target `Field` or `Method` reference and the required type.

This metadata is cached per bean class, so the reflection scan happens only once per type — even for prototype-scoped beans that are instantiated many times. The caching is important because Java reflection has real overhead: `Class.getDeclaredFields()` and `Class.getDeclaredMethods()` are not free operations, and calling them on every bean creation would add visible startup cost in large applications with thousands of beans.

sections.title: Type Resolution: What Happens When Multiple Beans Match
sections.content:
When `AutowiredAnnotationBeanPostProcessor` resolves an injection point, it asks the `BeanFactory` for all beans matching the declared type. The resolution follows a **strict fallback chain** that determines which bean gets injected.

**Step 1 — Type match.** Spring searches the registry for all beans assignable to the injection point's type. If exactly one match exists, it's injected immediately.

**Step 2 — Qualifier narrowing.** If multiple beans match the type, Spring checks for `@Qualifier("name")` on the injection point. If present, only the bean with the matching qualifier survives.

**Step 3 — Primary selection.** Without a qualifier, Spring looks for a bean marked `@Primary`. If exactly one primary exists among the candidates, it wins.

**Step 4 — Name fallback.** As a last resort, Spring compares the **field or parameter name** against bean names. If you have `private PaymentGateway stripeGateway`, Spring will match a bean named `stripeGateway` if no qualifier or primary resolved the ambiguity.

If none of these steps produce a single winner, Spring throws `NoUniqueBeanDefinitionException` at startup. This fail-fast behavior is deliberate — ambiguous injection is always a configuration error, not something to resolve silently.

sections.title: The Reflection Call: How Field.setAccessible(true) Bypasses Private Modifiers
sections.content:
For field injection, the actual wiring happens through Java reflection. The `AutowiredAnnotationBeanPostProcessor` calls `Field.setAccessible(true)` on the private field — this is the JVM's mechanism for bypassing access modifiers — and then calls `Field.set(bean, resolvedDependency)` to write the dependency directly into the field.

This is why field injection cannot work with `final` fields. Java's `final` field semantics guarantee that the value is set exactly once during construction. Reflection can technically write to a `final` field, but the JVM is allowed to inline the original value, meaning the write might not be visible to other code. The Java Memory Model makes this behavior **undefined**, which is why Spring doesn't attempt it.

Constructor injection sidesteps this entirely. Dependencies are resolved before the constructor runs and passed as arguments — no reflection on fields, no access modifier tricks. The resulting fields can be `final`, the object is fully immutable after construction, and the entire process is transparent to the JVM's optimization pipeline. This fundamental difference in the injection mechanism — constructor arguments vs reflective field writes — is what makes constructor injection the Spring team's recommended approach.

sections.title: Key Points
sections.content:
- **`AutowiredAnnotationBeanPostProcessor` — not magic, a BeanPostProcessor** — it's a concrete post-processor Spring registers automatically; it scans every bean for `@Autowired`, `@Value`, and `@Inject` then resolves and injects them.
- **Field-injected deps are `null` in the constructor body** — the BeanPostProcessor fires in `postProcessProperties`, after the constructor returns; reading an `@Autowired` field inside the constructor causes NPE.
- **Resolution order: type → `@Qualifier` → `@Primary` → field name** — Spring walks this fallback chain; if nothing resolves to exactly one bean, `NoUniqueBeanDefinitionException` fails startup.
- **`Field.setAccessible(true)` bypasses `private` — `final` is impossible** — reflection writes past access modifiers; the JVM's memory model leaves reflective writes to `final` fields as undefined behavior, so field injection can never use `final`.
- **Injection metadata is cached per class, not per instance** — the `Class.getDeclaredFields()` scan runs once per bean type; prototype beans created thousands of times pay the reflection cost only once.

sections.title: How to Answer This Verbally
sections.content:
When you annotate a field with `@Autowired`, Spring doesn't touch the compiler — it delegates to a `BeanPostProcessor` that runs after your object is constructed and uses Java reflection to write into private fields. That's the whole mechanism.

**The processor**
- `AutowiredAnnotationBeanPostProcessor` is registered automatically with `@SpringBootApplication`; it scans every bean class for `@Autowired`, `@Value`, and `@Inject`
- For constructor injection, this step is skipped — dependencies are resolved before the object exists and passed as arguments
- For field and setter injection, the processor fires in `postProcessProperties`, after the constructor returns — which is why `@Autowired` fields read inside a constructor body return `null`

**Type resolution**
- Spring searches for matching beans by type first; if exactly one matches, it is injected immediately
- With multiple type matches: `@Qualifier` narrows by name, `@Primary` picks the default, and field name is the last resort — none of these resolve to one? `NoUniqueBeanDefinitionException` fails startup

**The reflection call**
- `Field.setAccessible(true)` bypasses `private` modifiers; `Field.set(bean, resolvedDependency)` writes the value directly
- This is why field injection cannot use `final` — the JVM's memory model leaves reflective writes to `final` fields undefined; constructor injection avoids this entirely
- Injection metadata is cached per class so the reflection scan runs once per type, not once per prototype instance

Understanding this chain — BeanPostProcessor, type resolution, reflection — explains most of the my `@Autowired` is not working debugging sessions. Constructor injection sidesteps all of it.

sections.title: When Spring Finds Two Beans of the Same Type — and How @Qualifier and @Primary Break the Tie
sections.content:
The most common Spring startup error in any non-trivial application is `NoUniqueBeanDefinitionException` — Spring found multiple beans of the same type and doesn't know which one to inject. This happens naturally as applications grow: you add a second `DataSource` for a reporting database, a second `RestTemplate` with different timeouts, or a second `PaymentGateway` implementation for a new provider.

Spring's default behavior is strict — **if exactly one bean matches the required type, it's injected. If two or more match, Spring refuses to guess.** This fail-fast approach is deliberate: silently picking one would create bugs that only surface in production.

`@Primary` and `@Qualifier` are the two disambiguation mechanisms. **`@Primary` marks a default** — the bean Spring should choose when no other guidance is given. `@Qualifier` is explicit selection — the injection point names exactly which bean it wants. When both are present, `@Qualifier` wins because it's more specific. Understanding this precedence chain — and knowing that the field name itself is the last-resort fallback — is what interviewers are testing.

sections.title: How @Primary Sets the Default and @Qualifier Overrides It
The Field Name Fallback and Why Custom Qualifier Annotations Scale Better
Key Points
sections.content:
- **`@Qualifier` > `@Primary` > field name — resolution order matters** — when `@Qualifier` is present at the injection point, `@Primary` is completely ignored; field name is the silent last resort and breaks when you rename the variable.
- **`@Qualifier` value = bean name, lowercase first letter** — `@Qualifier("SmsNotifier")` fails at startup; the default bean name is the class name with a lowercase first character (`smsNotifier`); `@Component("customName")` overrides this.
- **`@Primary` on two beans of the same type results in `NoUniqueBeanDefinitionException`** — Spring does not pick between two primaries; it fails fast at startup.
- **Custom `@Qualifier` annotations = compile-time safety** — string-based `@Qualifier("stripe")` fails only at runtime on a typo; a `@Stripe` meta-annotation catches typos at compile time and survives refactoring.
- **Field name fallback is silent and fragile** — `private Notifier smsNotifier` matches a bean named `smsNotifier` without any annotation; rename the field and injection silently breaks.

sections.title: How to Answer This Verbally
sections.content:
When Spring finds multiple beans of the same type, it refuses to guess which one to inject — `NoUniqueBeanDefinitionException` at startup. `@Primary` and `@Qualifier` are the two tools that break the tie, and they follow a clear precedence order.

**`@Primary`**
- Marks the default candidate — any injection point that asks for `Notifier` by type gets `EmailNotifier` without needing a qualifier
- When `@Qualifier` is also present at the injection point, `@Qualifier` wins — it is more specific and completely overrides `@Primary`
- Putting `@Primary` on two beans of the same type does not resolve the ambiguity — Spring throws `NoUniqueBeanDefinitionException` again

**`@Qualifier`**
- Provides explicit selection at the injection point — names exactly which bean is wanted
- The value must match the bean name exactly, lowercase first letter — `@Qualifier("SmsNotifier")` produces a `NoSuchBeanDefinitionException`, not a type-match failure
- Custom qualifier annotations are type-safe: `@Stripe PaymentGateway gateway` — typos fail at compile time, not at deployment

The field name is Spring's last-resort fallback — declare `private Notifier smsNotifier` and Spring matches a bean named `smsNotifier` without any annotation. It works, but rename the field and injection silently breaks. Custom qualifier annotations are the production-ready approach for codebases with multiple implementations of the same interface.

questions.question: How does @Value work for injecting properties into Spring beans?

sections.title: Why Missing Properties Crash Your Application — and the One-Character Fix
sections.content:
`@Value` is the simplest way to get external configuration into a Spring bean — and it's also the most common source of startup failures for teams that don't know one syntax detail. When you write `@Value("${api.url}")` and `api.url` isn't defined in any property source, Spring doesn't inject null or an empty string. It throws `IllegalArgumentException` and your application refuses to start.

The fix is a single colon: `@Value("${api.url:}")` provides an empty string default. `@Value("${api.url:https://fallback.example.com}")` provides a meaningful fallback. This **colon syntax** is the difference between an application that explodes on missing configuration and one that degrades gracefully.

But `@Value` has a deeper scaling problem beyond defaults. It works fine for one or two properties, but past three related values — a URL, a timeout, a retry count — it becomes scattered and untestable. Each property is injected independently, validated nowhere, and documented nowhere. For structured configuration, `@ConfigurationProperties` is the proper tool: it binds a prefix to a POJO, validates at startup, and generates IDE auto-completion metadata.

The decision is simple: **`@Value` for isolated one-off values** (a feature flag, a secret key). **`@ConfigurationProperties` for anything with a prefix and more than two properties.**

sections.title: Property Placeholders: The ${} Syntax and Its Gotchas
SpEL Expressions: The #{} Syntax for Computed Values
When @Value Stops Scaling: The Migration to @ConfigurationProperties
Key Points
sections.content:
- **No colon means startup crash** — `@Value("${api.url}")` throws `IllegalArgumentException` if `api.url` is missing; `@Value("${api.url:}")` provides an empty default. One colon is the difference.
- **Space after colon injects the space** — `${key: default}` injects `" default"` with a leading space; always write `${key:default}` without spaces or URL and numeric parsing break silently.
- **Injected once at startup, never refreshed** — `@Value` resolves at bean creation and caches the result; property changes after startup have no effect without `@RefreshScope` (Spring Cloud).
- **`${}` inside `#{}`, never reversed** — `#{'${csv.values}'.split(',')}` applies SpEL to a resolved property; the reverse nesting order is invalid.
- **`@ConfigurationProperties` for three or more related properties** — groups a prefix into a POJO with JSR-303 validation, IDE auto-completion, and `Duration`/`DataSize` auto-conversion; migrate from `@Value` when a prefix appears.
- **SpEL in `@Value` fails at startup on error** — `SpelEvaluationException` at startup if the expression fails; keep SpEL simple, move complex logic to `@PostConstruct` where you can handle errors gracefully.

sections.title: How to Answer This Verbally
sections.content:
`@Value` is the simplest way to inject external configuration — and the easiest to get wrong. A missing key crashes at startup, a space after the colon silently poisons URLs, and injected values never update without a restart.

**The `${}` syntax**
- `@Value("${key}")` looks up the key in Spring's `Environment`; if missing, throws `IllegalArgumentException` and the application will not start
- Add a default with a colon: `@Value("${key:fallback}")` — no space after the colon, or the space becomes part of the injected value
- Resolution happens once at bean creation and is cached — live reload requires `@RefreshScope` from Spring Cloud

**The `#{}` SpEL syntax**
- SpEL expressions go in `#{}`; they can call methods, reference beans, and evaluate ternary operators
- Most common pattern: `#{'${csv}'.split(',')}` — `${}` resolves the property first, SpEL transforms it; always `${}` inside `#{}`, never reversed
- If the SpEL expression fails at startup, you get `SpelEvaluationException` — keep expressions simple and move complex logic to `@PostConstruct`

When you have three or more related properties sharing a prefix, switch to `@ConfigurationProperties`. It binds the entire prefix to a POJO, validates at startup with `@Valid`, and gives your IDE auto-completion for your custom properties. `@Value` for isolated one-off values; `@ConfigurationProperties` for anything with a prefix.

questions.question: What is the difference between @Component, @Service, @Repository, and @Controller?
questions.title: @Component vs @Service vs @Repository vs @Controller
questions.direct_answer: All four are stereotype annotations that mark a class as a Spring-managed component and trigger component-scan registration. The key difference is semantic clarity and, for @Repository specifically, automatic exception translation — Spring wraps persistence exceptions into its DataAccessException hierarchy.

interviewer_intent.testing: Whether the candidate knows these are not just aliases — @Repository has real runtime behavior and the others convey intent used by tools and AOP advisors.
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Saying all four are 'exactly the same' and missing the @Repository exception translation and the role of @Controller in Spring MVC dispatch.
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Mention that custom stereotypes can be built by composing @Component with your own annotation, and that Spring's persistence exception translation is applied via PersistenceExceptionTranslationPostProcessor.

sections.title: Why @Repository Is the Only One With Real Runtime Behavior
sections.content:
The most common interview mistake is saying all four annotations are identical. They're not — and the difference isn't just naming convention. All four are **meta-annotated with `@Component`**, which means component-scan discovers them equally. But `@Repository` and `@Controller` carry real framework behavior that `@Component` and `@Service` do not.

**`@Repository`** triggers `PersistenceExceptionTranslationPostProcessor`, which wraps the bean in a proxy that catches low-level persistence exceptions — `SQLException`, Hibernate's `JDBCException` — and rethrows them as Spring's `DataAccessException` hierarchy. This decouples your service layer from your ORM. Without `@Repository`, a `JDBCException` leaks through your service layer and your controller has to catch Hibernate-specific types.

**`@Controller`** tells Spring MVC's `DispatcherServlet` to scan the class for `@RequestMapping` methods. Without it (or `@RestController`), your endpoint methods won't be registered as HTTP handlers — the most confusing silent failure in Spring MVC.

`@Service` carries no runtime behavior today. It's a **semantic marker** that communicates intent: this class contains business logic. AOP pointcuts often target `@Service` classes for transaction management or logging, and architecture tools use it for dependency diagrams.

sections.title: What Each Stereotype Actually Does Beyond Component Scanning
sections.content:
The table shows that the four annotations differ on two axes: **runtime behavior** and **semantic intent**. Only `@Repository` and `@Controller` add framework-level processing that `@Component` doesn't provide.

| Annotation | Meta-annotation | Runtime Behavior | Semantic Intent |
|---|---|---|---|
| `@Component` | — (base) | Component scanning only | Generic managed bean |
| `@Service` | `@Component` | None beyond scanning | Business logic layer |
| `@Repository` | `@Component` | Exception translation (SQL → `DataAccessException`) | Data access layer |
| `@Controller` | `@Component` | MVC handler mapping (`@RequestMapping` discovery) | Web/presentation layer |
| `@RestController` | `@Controller` + `@ResponseBody` | Handler mapping + automatic JSON serialization | REST API layer |

The `@RestController` row is a common follow-up. It's `@Controller` plus `@ResponseBody` on every method — meaning return values are serialized to JSON/XML directly instead of being resolved as view names.

sections.title: Building Custom Stereotypes — Architecture Rules as Annotations
Why @Repository's Exception Translation Actually Matters in Production Code
sections.content:
Of the four stereotypes, only `@Repository` provides runtime behavior beyond lifecycle registration: **exception translation**. When `@Repository` is present, Spring wraps the bean in a `PersistenceExceptionTranslationPostProcessor` proxy. Any persistence exception thrown (JDBC `DataAccessException`, JPA `PersistenceException`, Hibernate exception) is **intercepted and translated** into Spring's `DataAccessException` hierarchy.

This matters because persistence exceptions are vendor-specific. A Hibernate `ConstraintViolationException` is different from JDBC's `SQLIntegrityConstraintViolationException` — both represent the same underlying failure but require different catch blocks if not translated. With `@Repository` translation, your service layer catches `DataIntegrityViolationException` (Spring's abstraction) regardless of whether the underlying database stack is JPA, JDBC, or MongoDB.

Without `@Repository` (or without the `PersistenceExceptionTranslationPostProcessor` bean), exceptions propagate as vendor-specific types — your service layer is coupled to the specific persistence technology. This violates the separation between persistence and business logic that `@Repository` is designed to enforce.

In Spring Boot applications, the `PersistenceExceptionTranslationPostProcessor` is auto-configured. In traditional Spring applications without autoconfiguration, you must explicitly declare this bean for `@Repository` exception translation to work. This is a common gap when migrating legacy Spring XML configurations to annotation-based configurations — the annotation is present but the exception translation doesn't happen because the post-processor wasn't declared.

The practical implication for **layered architecture**: if your JPA repository throws a `DataIntegrityViolationException` and your service layer catches `DataIntegrityViolationException`, you're depending on Spring's translated exception, not JPA's. This is the right design — your service layer stays decoupled from the ORM vendor. But if you ever remove `@Repository` from your repository class (easy to do when refactoring), exception translation stops, and callers that caught Spring's `DataAccessException` subclasses start seeing raw JPA exceptions. This silent breakage is another reason `@Repository` is not just a naming convention — it carries runtime behavior that the rest of the application may depend on.

sections.title: Key Points
sections.content:
- **`@Repository` is the only stereotype with real runtime behavior** — `PersistenceExceptionTranslationPostProcessor` wraps it in a proxy that translates SQL/JPA/Hibernate exceptions into Spring's `DataAccessException` hierarchy; the others are semantic markers only.
- **`@Controller` enables MVC handler mapping** — `DispatcherServlet` scans `@RequestMapping` methods only in `@Controller`-annotated classes; a REST endpoint on a plain `@Component` is silently ignored.
- **All four are meta-annotated with `@Component`** — component scan discovers all four equally; the difference is the additional framework behavior each carries, not how they are discovered.
- **`@Service` has no runtime behavior today** — it is a semantic marker for business logic; AOP pointcuts and architecture tools use it, but Spring itself treats it identically to `@Component`.
- **Custom stereotypes can compose behavior** — annotate your own annotation with `@Service` + `@Transactional` to create a `@UseCase` that registers as a bean and gets transaction management automatically.

sections.title: How to Answer This Verbally
sections.content:
All four annotations — `@Component`, `@Service`, `@Repository`, `@Controller` — are meta-annotated with `@Component`, so component scan discovers them all equally. The difference is not how they are found, it is what each one adds on top of basic bean registration.

**`@Repository`**
- The only stereotype with real runtime behavior: a `PersistenceExceptionTranslationPostProcessor` proxy wraps it
- That proxy intercepts Hibernate, JPA, and JDBC exceptions and rethrows them as Spring's `DataAccessException` hierarchy — your service layer catches one consistent exception type regardless of the ORM vendor
- Remove `@Repository` and exceptions leak as vendor-specific types through the service layer

**`@Controller`**
- Tells Spring MVC's `DispatcherServlet` to scan the class for `@RequestMapping` methods
- Without it, your `@GetMapping` endpoint is silently ignored — the most confusing silent failure in Spring MVC
- `@RestController` = `@Controller` + `@ResponseBody` on every method

**`@Service` and `@Component`**
- `@Service` carries no runtime behavior — it is a semantic marker for the business logic layer
- AOP pointcuts and architecture analysis tools use it to identify the business layer

Start with `@Component` for generic beans, `@Service` for business logic, `@Repository` for data access (and get the exception translation benefit), `@Controller` for web endpoints. The naming communicates intent to every developer who reads the code.

questions.question: @ComponentScan — How Spring Discovers Beans
questions.title: @ComponentScan — How Spring Discovers Beans

sections.title: Why Your @Service Bean Wasn't Found — The Package Scan Boundary Problem
sections.content:
The most common Spring startup mystery is: 'I annotated my class with `@Service` but Spring says it doesn't exist.' The answer is almost always **component scanning didn't reach that package**.

`@ComponentScan` tells Spring which packages to scan for stereotype annotations — `@Component`, `@Service`, `@Repository`, `@Controller`, and anything meta-annotated with `@Component`. Without it, Spring doesn't know your beans exist. With `@SpringBootApplication`, you get `@ComponentScan` automatically — but it **only scans the package of the main class and all sub-packages**.

This means if your main class is in `com.example.app` and a service lives in `com.example.common.utils`, that service won't be discovered. Not because the annotation is wrong, but because the scanner never looked there. Understanding the scan boundary — and knowing how to extend it without creating a maintenance headache — is what this question tests.

The scanning process itself uses ASM bytecode reading — not class loading — to inspect annotations. This means Spring can evaluate thousands of classes without loading them into the JVM, which keeps startup fast even with broad scan boundaries.

One important nuance: `@ComponentScan` is inherited by `@SpringBootApplication`, but you can still use `@ComponentScan` explicitly on additional `@Configuration` classes to scan supplementary packages. When multiple `@ComponentScan` configurations exist in the same context, Spring merges them — both sets of packages are scanned. This is how multi-module projects can have each module's `@Configuration` class declare its own local scan, and the root application class compose them.

sections.title: How @SpringBootApplication Sets the Default Scan Boundary
Filters: Include, Exclude, and Why Scanning Too Broadly Causes Problems
sections.content:
`@ComponentScan` supports **include and exclude filters** that control which classes are registered even within scanned packages. This is useful for test configurations, multi-module projects, and preventing accidental bean registration.

```java
@ComponentScan(
    basePackages = "com.example",
    excludeFilters = @ComponentScan.Filter(
        type = FilterType.REGEX,
        pattern = "com\\.example\\.legacy\\..*"
    )
)
```

The filter types include `ANNOTATION` (exclude classes with a specific annotation), `ASSIGNABLE_TYPE` (exclude specific classes), `REGEX` (pattern-based), and `CUSTOM` (your own `TypeFilter` implementation). The `ANNOTATION` filter is the most common — for example, excluding `@Configuration` classes from a shared library that you want to import selectively.

A real-world pattern is **test isolation**. In integration tests, you might exclude certain beans that connect to external services and replace them with test doubles. `@SpringBootTest` combined with `@ComponentScan(excludeFilters = ...)` gives you precise control over which beans participate in the test context.

sections.title: Lazy Scanning, Index-Based Discovery, and the Performance Cost of Scanning Every Class in a Large Monolith
sections.content:
Component scanning works by loading every class on the classpath within the scanned packages, reading their annotations, and registering annotated classes as beans. In small projects with a few hundred classes, this is imperceptible. In a large monolith with thousands of classes, scanning can add seconds to startup time.

**`spring-context-indexer`** generates a compile-time index (`META-INF/spring.components`) listing all annotated components. At startup, Spring reads the index instead of scanning class files — dramatically faster for large codebases. Add the dependency as an annotation processor; no code changes required.

For **multi-module projects**, each module can define its own `@Configuration` class with a precise `@ComponentScan` restricted to that module's package. The root application class combines them with `@Import({ModuleAConfig.class, ModuleBConfig.class})` or relies on Spring Boot's `@SpringBootApplication` combined with module-specific auto-configuration.

**Excluding test infrastructure classes from production scans** is a common need. `@ComponentScan(excludeFilters = @ComponentScan.Filter(type = FilterType.ANNOTATION, classes = TestConfiguration.class))` prevents test-only beans from being registered in production contexts. This is essential when test helper beans (fake implementations, in-memory repositories) live in the `src/test` directory but are otherwise reachable from production classpath configurations in integration test setups.

The scanning order matters when multiple `@Configuration` classes with `@ComponentScan` are present. Spring processes them in declaration order within the configuration hierarchy — a source of subtle 'bean already defined' conflicts when two configurations accidentally scan overlapping packages.

**Detecting scan performance issues** is straightforward with `--debug` mode. The conditions evaluation report shows which configuration classes were processed and how many beans were registered. If startup is slow, the `ApplicationStartup` tracking API (Spring Boot 2.4+) lets you add `SpringApplication.setApplicationStartup(BufferingApplicationStartup)` and then query `/actuator/startup` to see exactly how long each scan and bean creation phase takes. Broad scans across packages with many classes are the most common startup performance culprit in large codebases.

sections.title: Key Points
sections.content:
- **`@SpringBootApplication` scans only the package of the main class and sub-packages** — a service in `com.example.common.utils` is invisible if the main class is in `com.example.app`; this is the most common root cause of bean-not-found errors.
- **Scanning uses ASM bytecode reading, not class loading** — Spring inspects annotations without loading classes into the JVM; broad scans stay fast but still add time when the scanned package tree is very large.
- **`spring-context-indexer` generates a compile-time component index** — adds `META-INF/spring.components` listing all annotated components; at startup Spring reads the index instead of scanning class files — measurable speedup in large monoliths.
- **`excludeFilters` prevents test beans from leaking into production** — `FilterType.ANNOTATION` can exclude `@TestConfiguration` classes that live on the test classpath.
- **Multiple `@ComponentScan` definitions are merged** — Spring combines all scanned packages from all `@Configuration` classes; overlapping packages cause duplicate bean definition conflicts.

sections.title: How to Answer This Verbally
sections.content:
Spring can only inject beans it knows about — and it only knows about beans in packages it scanned. That single fact explains most of the I annotated my class but Spring says it does not exist debugging sessions.

**The default scan boundary**

sections.title: Why Singleton Doesn't Mean Thread-Safe — and Why Prototype Doesn't Mean Disposable
sections.content:
Spring's default scope is **singleton** — one instance per `ApplicationContext`, shared by every injection point. Most developers stop there and never think about scope again. But there are two misconceptions that cause real bugs.

First, **singleton does not mean thread-safe**. Spring creates one instance and hands the same reference to every thread. If that bean has mutable state — a field that changes between requests — every concurrent request sees and modifies the same field. Race conditions are invisible until they produce corrupted data in production.

Second, **prototype scope means Spring creates a new instance every time the bean is requested** — but Spring does not manage the full lifecycle. There's no `@PreDestroy` call, no destruction callback. If a prototype bean opens a database connection, Spring won't close it. Cleanup is your responsibility.

The web scopes — `request` and `session` — exist specifically for stateful web interactions where the state must be isolated per HTTP request or per user session. But injecting a request-scoped bean into a singleton creates a subtle problem that requires **scoped proxies** to solve.

sections.content:
Spring's default scope is singleton — one instance per `ApplicationContext`, shared across all threads. Most developers never change this and assume it means safe. Two misconceptions cause real bugs.

**Singleton**
- One instance per container, shared across all threads — mutable state in a singleton bean is a race condition waiting to happen
- Full lifecycle: Spring calls `@PostConstruct` and `@PreDestroy`; the bean lives for the entire application lifetime

**Prototype**
- New instance every time the bean is injected or `getBean()` is called — isolated, no sharing between threads
- Spring creates but never destroys prototype beans; `@PreDestroy` is never called; if the prototype holds a database connection or file handle, the calling code must close it

**Request and Session scopes**
- One instance per HTTP request or per HTTP session — correct for per-user or per-request state
- Injecting a request-scoped bean into a singleton is the most common scope trap: the singleton is created at startup before any request exists; Spring throws `BeanCreationException: no thread-bound request found`
- Fix: `@Scope(value="request", proxyMode=ScopedProxyMode.TARGET_CLASS)` — Spring injects a CGLIB proxy; each method call resolves the real request-scoped bean from the current thread

Use singleton for stateless services (the default), prototype when you need isolated mutable state per use, request/session for web-specific state. Never store per-request state in a singleton field.

questions.question: What happens when you inject a prototype-scoped bean into a singleton bean?

sections.title: The Injection That Happens Once When You Expected It to Happen Every Time
sections.content:
Injecting a prototype-scoped bean into a singleton is one of Spring's most common traps. The developer expects a **fresh instance** on every use — that's why they chose prototype scope. But Spring injects the prototype once during the singleton's construction, and the singleton holds that same instance forever. The prototype becomes a de facto singleton, defeating the entire purpose of prototype scope.

The root cause is a scope mismatch. Singleton beans are created once and their dependencies are injected once. When a prototype bean is declared as a constructor or field dependency of a singleton, Spring resolves it during singleton creation, creates one prototype instance, and injects it. From that point on, the singleton holds a fixed reference. No mechanism exists to "re-inject" the field later.

This manifests as a concurrency bug or a state leak. A prototype bean is typically used because it holds per-use state — a request tracker, a parser with internal buffers, a computation context. When it's shared across threads via a singleton, that per-use state is corrupted. Two concurrent requests write to the same object, and the output is a mixture of both requests' data.

The fix is to avoid holding a prototype as a field entirely. Instead, ask Spring for a new instance each time you need one. Spring provides three mechanisms for this: `ObjectProvider<T>`, `ObjectFactory<T>`, and `@Lookup` method injection. `ObjectProvider` is the recommended approach because it's type-safe, well-documented, and doesn't require CGLIB subclassing.

The bug manifests differently depending on whether the singleton is used by a single thread or many. In single-threaded scenarios (like a command-line batch application), the singleton reuses the same prototype instance on every invocation — state accumulates from previous runs. In multi-threaded web applications, concurrent requests share the prototype's mutable state, producing data corruption that appears intermittently and is nearly impossible to reproduce in isolation.

sections.title: ObjectProvider: The Clean Fix for Scope Mismatch
Three Solutions to Scope Mismatch — And Why Each Has Different Trade-offs
sections.content:
When a prototype bean is injected into a singleton, the prototype's state is shared across all uses of the singleton — defeating the purpose of prototype scope. Spring provides three solutions, each with different trade-offs.

**`ObjectProvider<T>` (recommended):** Inject `ObjectProvider<PrototypeBean>` and call `.getObject()` each time you need a new instance. The provider is singleton-scoped, but each `getObject()` call creates a new prototype instance. This is the cleanest solution — no AOP proxy, no container coupling, testable without Spring.

**Scoped proxy (`@Scope(proxyMode = ScopedProxyMode.TARGET_CLASS)`):** Spring wraps the prototype bean in a CGLIB proxy. Every call through the proxy creates a new prototype instance. The singleton receives the proxy instead of a real instance — from its perspective, the dependency is 'always there', but the proxy creates fresh instances per call. This works transparently but requires CGLIB bytecode manipulation and adds complexity visible in debugging sessions (stack traces show proxy classes).

**`ApplicationContext.getBean()`:** Call `getBean(PrototypeBean.class)` each time you need an instance. This works but couples your class to the Spring container — a `BeanFactory` dependency in business logic is a code smell. It's acceptable in infrastructure code (factories, adapters) where Spring dependency is already explicit.

For **thread-safe stateful beans**, consider whether prototype scope is actually the right solution. If the state is request-specific, request scope (`@Scope("request")`) in a web application may be more appropriate. If the state is conversation-specific (multi-step flow), session scope makes more sense. Prototype is correct when each calling component needs a truly independent instance with independent mutable state.

A design-level question worth asking before reaching for prototype scope: **does this bean need to be a Spring bean at all?** If the only reason it's a Spring bean is that it has dependencies, but you want a fresh instance every time, consider a factory bean or builder pattern that creates new instances directly. A factory method annotated `@Bean @Scope("prototype")` works, but sometimes `new MyObject(injectedDep)` with the dependency constructor-injected into the factory is cleaner. Prototype scope adds complexity that's only justified when the bean itself needs the full Spring lifecycle — `@PostConstruct`, AOP wrapping, `@Autowired` dependencies on the prototype itself.

sections.title: Key Points
sections.content:
- **Prototype injected into singleton becomes a singleton** — Spring injects the prototype exactly once during singleton construction; the singleton holds that same instance forever, defeating prototype scope.
- **`ObjectProvider<T>` is the clean fix** — inject `ObjectProvider<PrototypeBean>` and call `.getObject()` each time you need a fresh instance; the provider is singleton-scoped, creation happens at call time.
- **`ApplicationContext.getBean()` works but is a code smell** — coupling business logic to the Spring API is an anti-pattern; use `ObjectProvider` or `@Lookup` instead.
- **`@Lookup` method injection uses CGLIB** — Spring subclasses the singleton and overrides the annotated abstract method to return a new prototype instance; no field, no provider dependency, but requires CGLIB subclassing.
- **Spring never calls `@PreDestroy` on prototype instances** — resource cleanup is the caller's responsibility regardless of how the prototype was obtained.

sections.title: Why the Order of Six Lifecycle Phases Matters — and Where Most Bugs Hide
sections.content:
The Spring IoC container manages each bean through a precise lifecycle. Hooks are provided at every stage so you can plug in custom logic — from property overrides to proxy wrapping to resource cleanup.

The Spring Bean lifecycle is a precisely ordered sequence of callbacks that gives developers hooks at every critical transition. Understanding it demonstrates senior-level Spring knowledge.

**Phase 1 — Instantiation:** The container uses the bean's constructor (or a factory method) to create the raw Java object. At this point, no dependencies have been injected — fields are null. If constructor injection is used, dependencies are resolved and provided as constructor arguments during this phase.

**Phase 2 — Dependency Injection:** After instantiation, Spring injects dependencies via setter methods or field injection (`@Autowired`). The `AutowiredAnnotationBeanPostProcessor` handles `@Autowired`, `@Value`, and `@Inject` annotations. If a required dependency cannot be resolved, the context fails to start.

**Phase 3 — Post-Construction Callbacks:** `@PostConstruct` methods (or `InitializingBean.afterPropertiesSet()`) run after all dependencies are injected. This is the safest place for initialization logic that depends on injected beans — connection pool warmup, cache population, or validation. `@PostConstruct` runs before `BeanPostProcessor.postProcessAfterInitialization`.

**Phase 4 — BeanPostProcessor:** Spring iterates over all registered `BeanPostProcessor` implementations and calls `postProcessBeforeInitialization` and `postProcessAfterInitialization` on every bean. This is how AOP proxies are created (`AnnotationAwareAspectJAutoProxyCreator`), `@Scheduled` methods are registered, and `@Async` methods are wrapped. After this phase, the bean may be a proxy rather than the original object.

**Phase 5 — In Use:** The bean serves application requests. Singleton beans live for the entire application lifetime. Prototype beans are handed off and the container does not manage them further.

**Phase 6 — Destruction:** When the context shuts down, `@PreDestroy` methods (or `DisposableBean.destroy()`) run on singleton beans. This is where you close connections, flush caches, and release external resources. Prototype beans do not receive destruction callbacks because the container does not track them.

sections.title: Instantiation and Injection: Where Constructor Code Can't See @Autowired Fields
Post-Construction Callbacks: @PostConstruct vs InitializingBean vs @Bean(initMethod)
sections.content:
After injection completes, Spring fires **initialization callbacks** in a specific order. If a bean implements multiple callback mechanisms, they execute in this sequence: `@PostConstruct` first, then `InitializingBean.afterPropertiesSet()`, then the custom `initMethod` declared in `@Bean(initMethod = "setup")`.

**`@PostConstruct`** is the modern standard — a JSR-250 annotation that marks a method to run once after all dependencies are injected. It's clean, framework-agnostic (works outside Spring), and clearly communicates intent. Use it for connection pool warm-up, cache preloading, or any setup that requires injected collaborators.

**`InitializingBean`** is Spring's older interface approach. Implementing `afterPropertiesSet()` couples your class to the Spring API, which makes it harder to reuse outside the container. It still appears in Spring's own codebase and in legacy applications but is not recommended for new code.

**`@Bean(initMethod = "setup")`** is useful when you don't control the class source — third-party libraries whose beans need initialization. You specify the method name as a string in the `@Bean` declaration, and Spring calls it via reflection after injection.

A practical rule: use `@PostConstruct` for your own classes, `initMethod` for third-party classes, and avoid `InitializingBean` unless you're extending Spring's own framework code.

sections.title: BeanPostProcessor: The Hook That Creates Proxies for @Transactional and @Cacheable
sections.content:
After initialization callbacks complete, Spring invokes `BeanPostProcessor` implementations. These are the most powerful lifecycle extension point — they can inspect, modify, or **replace** the bean entirely.

The `BeanPostProcessor` interface defines two methods: `postProcessBeforeInitialization(bean, name)` runs before `@PostConstruct`, and `postProcessAfterInitialization(bean, name)` runs after. The 'after' hook is where **proxy creation** happens.

When you annotate a method with `@Transactional`, Spring's `AbstractAutoProxyCreator` — a `BeanPostProcessor` — detects it during the 'after' phase. Instead of returning the original bean, it returns a **CGLIB or JDK dynamic proxy** that wraps the original. Every external call to the bean goes through the proxy, which manages the transaction lifecycle.

This is why **self-invocation bypasses `@Transactional`**. When a method inside the bean calls another method on `this`, it bypasses the proxy and hits the original object directly — no transaction management, no caching, no aspect. The proxy only intercepts calls that come through the injected reference.

The same mechanism powers `@Cacheable`, `@Async`, `@Retry`, and every other annotation-driven aspect in Spring. Understanding that these work through post-processing proxies explains most of the 'why doesn't my annotation work?' debugging scenarios.

sections.title: Destruction: @PreDestroy Runs for Singletons But Not for Prototypes
Key Points
sections.content:
- **`@Autowired` fields are null in the constructor** — field injection fires in `postProcessProperties` after construction, not during; use constructor injection or move initialization to `@PostConstruct`.
- **Initialization callback order: `@PostConstruct` then `afterPropertiesSet()` then `initMethod`** — when a bean implements multiple mechanisms, they fire in this sequence; `@PostConstruct` always runs first.
- **`BeanPostProcessor.postProcessAfterInitialization` creates proxies** — `@Transactional`, `@Async`, and `@Cacheable` replace the original bean with a CGLIB proxy here; what other beans inject may be a proxy, not the original class.
- **`@PreDestroy` is never called on prototype beans** — Spring does not track prototype instances after creation; resource cleanup is the caller's responsibility.
- **`BeanFactoryPostProcessor` modifies bean definitions; `BeanPostProcessor` modifies bean instances** — `PropertySourcesPlaceholderConfigurer` is a `BeanFactoryPostProcessor`; `AutowiredAnnotationBeanPostProcessor` is a `BeanPostProcessor`.
- **Destruction runs in reverse creation order** — singletons are destroyed before the beans they depend on, guaranteeing clean shutdown sequencing.

sections.title: How to Answer This Verbally
sections.content:
The Spring bean lifecycle is a precisely ordered sequence of phases. Every annotation-driven feature — `@Autowired`, `@PostConstruct`, `@Transactional`, `@PreDestroy` — fires at a specific point in that sequence. Knowing the order explains the bugs.

**Instantiation and injection**
- Constructor injection: dependencies are resolved first, then the constructor runs — the object is fully wired from line one
- Field/setter injection: the constructor runs first (no-arg), then `AutowiredAnnotationBeanPostProcessor` fires in `postProcessProperties` — `@Autowired` fields are null inside the constructor body

**Initialization callbacks — in this order**
- `@PostConstruct` fires first — the safe place for startup logic that depends on injected collaborators
- `InitializingBean.afterPropertiesSet()` fires second — Spring's older interface approach, avoid in new code
- `@Bean(initMethod)` fires last — for third-party classes you cannot annotate

**`BeanPostProcessor` — where proxies are created**
- `postProcessAfterInitialization` runs after all callbacks; it can return a different object
- This is how `@Transactional`, `@Async`, and `@Cacheable` replace the bean with a CGLIB proxy
- Self-invocation via `this` bypasses the proxy — which is why `@Transactional` on an internal call does not work

**Destruction**
- `@PreDestroy` runs on singletons in reverse creation order when the context shuts down
- Prototype beans are handed off and never get `@PreDestroy` — Spring cannot call what it does not track

sections.title: Why You Can't Use @Autowired Fields in the Constructor — and What @PostConstruct Fixes
sections.content:
The problem `@PostConstruct` solves is a **timing gap** in the bean lifecycle. When Spring creates a bean, the constructor runs first. If the bean uses field injection, `@Autowired` fields are `null` during the constructor — they haven't been injected yet. Any initialization logic that depends on injected collaborators fails with `NullPointerException`.

`@PostConstruct` marks a method that Spring calls **after dependency injection is complete** but before the bean is put into service. It's the safe place for startup logic: warming caches, validating configuration, opening connections, or registering listeners.

`@PreDestroy` is the mirror — it runs when the `ApplicationContext` shuts down, giving the bean a chance to release resources cleanly. Close connection pools, flush buffers, deregister from external services. Together, these two annotations cover the **initialization and cleanup** that constructors and finalizers can't handle reliably.

The important caveat is scope. **`@PreDestroy` only runs for singleton beans.** Spring doesn't track prototype instances after creation — there's no shutdown hook, no destruction callback. If a prototype bean acquires resources, the calling code must close them explicitly.

Key Points
sections.content:
- **`@PostConstruct` is the safe place for initialization** — all `@Autowired` dependencies are fully injected when it runs; the constructor is not safe for field-injected deps.
- **Callback order: `@PostConstruct` then `afterPropertiesSet()` then `initMethod`** — when multiple mechanisms exist on one bean, they fire in this sequence.
- **`@PreDestroy` never fires on prototype beans** — Spring does not track prototype instances after creation; switching a singleton to prototype without adding explicit cleanup causes resource leaks.
- **`@Bean(destroyMethod="")` prevents auto-detected cleanup** — Spring auto-infers `destroyMethod` as `close()` or `shutdown()` for `@Bean` methods; set it to empty string to disable if auto-detection causes problems.

sections.content:
`@PostConstruct` and `@PreDestroy` exist because constructors and finalizers cannot reliably handle initialization and cleanup in a dependency-injected world.

**Why the constructor is not enough**
- With field injection, `@Autowired` fields are null inside the constructor — they have not been injected yet
- `@PostConstruct` runs after all injection is complete — it is the correct place to warm caches, validate configuration, open connections, or register listeners that depend on injected collaborators

**Callback order when all three exist on one bean**
- `@PostConstruct` fires first — JSR-250 standard, works in any Jakarta EE container, not just Spring
- `InitializingBean.afterPropertiesSet()` fires second — Spring's older interface approach; avoid in new code, it couples to the Spring API
- `@Bean(initMethod = "setup")` fires last — useful for third-party classes you cannot annotate

**`@PreDestroy` — cleanup on shutdown**
- Runs on singleton beans in reverse creation order when `ApplicationContext.close()` is called
- Never called on prototype beans — Spring does not track prototype instances after creation
- Switch a singleton to prototype scope without adding explicit cleanup and connections or threads leak silently

The practical rule: use `@PostConstruct` for your own classes, `@Bean(initMethod)` for third-party beans, and `@PreDestroy` to release any resource the bean acquired during initialization.

sections.title: The Extension Point That Powers Every Annotation You Use
sections.content:
`BeanPostProcessor` is the most important internal interface in Spring — and the one that developers least understand. Every major annotation-driven feature in Spring is implemented as a `BeanPostProcessor`: `@Autowired` is handled by `AutowiredAnnotationBeanPostProcessor`, `@Transactional` creates proxies via `InfrastructureAdvisorAutoProxyCreator`, `@Async` is processed by `AsyncAnnotationBeanPostProcessor`, `@Scheduled` by `ScheduledAnnotationBeanPostProcessor`.

A `BeanPostProcessor` intercepts every bean during creation, right between dependency injection and the bean being "ready." It has two hooks: `postProcessBeforeInitialization()` runs before `@PostConstruct`, and `postProcessAfterInitialization()` runs after. The "after" hook is particularly powerful because it can **replace the bean instance** — this is how Spring creates proxies for `@Transactional` and AOP.

Understanding this mechanism explains several behaviors that mystify developers. Why does `this.method()` bypass `@Transactional`? Because `@Transactional` works through a proxy wrapping the bean — `this` refers to the original instance, not the proxy. Why does `@Autowired` injection happen before `@PostConstruct`? Because `AutowiredAnnotationBeanPostProcessor` runs in the "before" hook, and `@PostConstruct` is the initialization callback that follows.

The interface is deceptively simple — two methods that receive a bean and return it (or a replacement). The complexity lies in knowing when to use it and understanding the ordering constraints with other post-processors.

sections.title: The Two Hooks: Before and After Initialization
Registration Timing: Why BeanPostProcessors Must Be Registered Early
sections.content:
`BeanPostProcessor` instances must be registered before the beans they need to process. Spring detects `BeanPostProcessor` beans during context refresh and registers them before creating any "normal" beans. This means a `BeanPostProcessor` cannot depend on beans that it's supposed to process — circular dependency.

There's also `BeanFactoryPostProcessor`, which is a fundamentally different extension point. While `BeanPostProcessor` processes bean instances after creation, `BeanFactoryPostProcessor` processes **bean definitions** before any bean is created. It can modify bean metadata — change scope, add property values, register new bean definitions entirely.

The distinction matters: `BeanFactoryPostProcessor` modifies the **blueprint** (bean definitions). `BeanPostProcessor` modifies the **product** (bean instances). `PropertySourcesPlaceholderConfigurer` (which resolves `${...}` placeholders) is a `BeanFactoryPostProcessor` — it modifies bean definitions to replace placeholder strings with actual values before any bean is instantiated.

`@Configuration` classes that declare `BeanFactoryPostProcessor` beans should use `static` `@Bean` methods. Non-static methods require the `@Configuration` class to be instantiated first, which forces early initialization of the configuration class and all its dependencies — potentially skipping other post-processors that haven't been registered yet. The `static` keyword avoids this ordering problem.

sections.title: Why Eager Initialization Is Usually Better — and When @Lazy Actually Helps
sections.content:
Spring's default behavior is **eager initialization** — all singleton beans are created at startup, before the application handles any requests. This is deliberate: configuration errors, missing dependencies, and circular references surface immediately instead of blowing up on the first user request.

`@Lazy` changes this to **on-demand initialization** — the bean is created the first time it's actually needed. This sounds like an optimization, but it's a trade-off. You gain faster startup at the cost of **deferred failure detection**. A miswired `@Lazy` bean won't throw `NoSuchBeanDefinitionException` at startup — it'll throw it on the first request that triggers its creation.

The legitimate use cases for `@Lazy` are narrow: beans that are **expensive to create** and **not always needed** (a reporting engine that's only used on Sundays), beans involved in **circular dependency breaking** (a temporary fix, not a design solution), and beans that depend on **runtime state** not available at startup (request-scoped resources).

For most applications, the startup time saved by `@Lazy` is measured in milliseconds — not worth the risk of runtime failures.

sections.title: How @Lazy Works: The Proxy That Delays Creation Until First Use
The Circular Dependency Hack: Why @Lazy Masks a Design Problem
sections.content:
The most common use of `@Lazy` in production codebases is **breaking circular dependencies**. When `ServiceA` depends on `ServiceB` and `ServiceB` depends on `ServiceA`, constructor injection throws `BeanCurrentlyInCreationException`. Adding `@Lazy` to one side creates a proxy that defers creation, breaking the cycle.

This works, but it's a **band-aid**. The circular dependency is a design smell — two classes that depend on each other usually share a responsibility that should be extracted into a third class, or the interaction should be decoupled through events or an interface.

The danger of `@Lazy` as a circular dependency fix is that it hides the problem. The code compiles, the tests pass, but the design issue remains. When someone later refactors one of the classes, the `@Lazy` annotation seems arbitrary and gets removed — resurfacing the original `BeanCurrentlyInCreationException`. At that point, nobody remembers why it was there.

**The proper fix** is to extract the shared concern, use `ApplicationEventPublisher` for decoupled communication, or restructure the dependency graph. Use `@Lazy` for circular dependencies only as a temporary workaround with a `// TODO: fix circular dependency` comment.

sections.title: Key Points
sections.content:
- **`@Lazy` defers creation but not failure detection** — a misconfigured `@Lazy` bean does not fail at startup; it fails on the first request that triggers its creation — a production failure instead of a deployment failure.
- **Spring injects a CGLIB proxy, not the real bean** — when a dependency is `@Lazy`, the injection point receives a proxy; the real bean is created on the first proxy method call.
- **`@Lazy` as a circular dependency fix is a design smell** — it breaks the cycle by deferring one side but hides the SRP violation; the `BeanCurrentlyInCreationException` returns when someone removes the annotation during refactoring.
- **The legitimate use cases are narrow** — expensive beans only needed occasionally (reporting engines), beans with runtime-state dependencies not available at startup.
- **`@Lazy` on the injection point parameter, not the bean class** — parameter-level placement gives fine-grained control; one consumer gets a lazy proxy while another gets the real bean eagerly.

sections.title: Why Circular Dependencies Are a Design Problem, Not a Framework Problem
sections.content:
A circular dependency means `ServiceA` needs `ServiceB` to be created, and `ServiceB` needs `ServiceA` to be created — a deadlock that Spring can't resolve for constructor injection. The temptation is to find a framework workaround (`@Lazy`, setter injection). The correct response is to **fix the design**.

Circular dependencies almost always signal a **Single Responsibility violation** — two classes that share a concern which should be extracted into a third class. Or they signal **missing abstraction** — the classes should communicate through events or an interface instead of direct references.

Spring's behavior depends on the injection style. **Constructor injection throws `BeanCurrentlyInCreationException` at startup** — fast and visible. Field and setter injection resolve the cycle silently using early references (Spring injects a partially-constructed bean), which can produce subtle runtime bugs when the partially-constructed bean is used before its dependencies are fully wired.

Spring Boot 2.6+ made this stricter by **disabling circular dependency resolution by default**. Even field-injected cycles now throw at startup unless you explicitly opt in with `spring.main.allow-circular-references=true`. This change reflects the community consensus that circular dependencies should be fixed, not tolerated.

sections.title: The BeanCurrentlyInCreationException: How to Read the Stack Trace
sections.content:
When Spring detects a circular dependency with constructor injection, the error message names the beans involved. The typical message looks like: 'Requested bean is currently in creation: Is there an unresolvable circular reference?'

The stack trace shows the dependency chain: Spring tries to create `ServiceA`, which requires `ServiceB`, which requires `ServiceA` — and `ServiceA` is already being created. The chain can be longer: A → B → C → A.

The fix starts with **understanding why both classes need each other**. Usually one of these patterns is the root cause:

**Pattern 1: Shared responsibility.** `OrderService` calls `InventoryService.reserve()`, and `InventoryService` calls `OrderService.getOrder()`. Both services handle order-related logic — extract an `OrderRepository` that both depend on instead of depending on each other.

**Pattern 2: Event-worthy interaction.** `PaymentService` notifies `NotificationService` of a payment, and `NotificationService` queries `PaymentService` for details. Replace the direct call with an `ApplicationEvent` — `PaymentService` publishes a `PaymentCompleted` event, and `NotificationService` listens for it. No mutual dependency.

- **`spring.main.allow-circular-references=true` is the escape hatch, not the fix** — enabling it acknowledges the design problem and defers it; the community consensus is to eliminate circular dependencies, not tolerate them.
- **Root cause is almost always SRP violation** — two classes that depend on each other share logic that belongs in a third class.
- **Fix 1: extract the shared concern** — create class C that both A and B depend on instead of depending on each other.
- **Fix 2: replace one direction with events** — `ApplicationEventPublisher` breaks the mutual dependency; A publishes, B listens, one-way dependency remains.
- **`@Lazy` breaks the cycle but hides the problem** — use only as a temporary workaround with a comment explaining why; it causes `BeanCurrentlyInCreationException` to resurface when someone removes it during refactoring.
