questions.question: What is the difference between BeanFactory and ApplicationContext in Spring?
questions.title: Spring IoC Container: BeanFactory vs ApplicationContext
questions.direct_answer: BeanFactory is Spring's root IoC interface providing basic dependency injection, while ApplicationContext extends it with enterprise features: event publishing, internationalization, AOP auto-proxying, and eager singleton initialization. In practice you almost always use ApplicationContext — BeanFactory exists mainly for constrained environments or when absolute minimal startup cost is required.

interviewer_intent.testing: Understanding of the Spring container hierarchy and why ApplicationContext is the default choice.
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Thinking they are interchangeable drop-in replacements, or not knowing that BeanFactory initializes beans lazily by default while ApplicationContext initializes singletons eagerly on startup.
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Mention that ApplicationContext implements several sub-interfaces (MessageSource, ApplicationEventPublisher, ResourceLoader) which gives it the extra capabilities, and name concrete implementations like ClassPathXmlApplicationContext or AnnotationConfigApplicationContext.

sections.title: Why BeanFactory Still Exists When Everyone Uses ApplicationContext
sections.content:
Every Spring application uses `ApplicationContext` — it's what `SpringApplication.run()` creates, what `@SpringBootTest` loads, and what you interact with when you call `context.getBean()`. So why does `BeanFactory` still exist?

**`BeanFactory` is the root interface** — it defines the core contract for any Spring container: register beans, resolve dependencies, manage lifecycle. `ApplicationContext` extends `BeanFactory` and adds everything else: event publishing, internationalization, environment abstraction, resource loading, and AOP auto-proxying.

The practical difference is **initialization strategy**. `BeanFactory` initializes beans lazily — a bean is created only when first requested. `ApplicationContext` eagerly creates all singleton beans at startup. Eager initialization catches configuration errors immediately instead of failing on the first request in production.

You'll encounter `BeanFactory` directly only in two situations: writing custom `BeanPostProcessor` or `BeanFactoryPostProcessor` implementations that need the lower-level API, or in memory-constrained environments where lazy initialization is necessary to reduce startup footprint. The relationship is one of specialization — `ApplicationContext` is a `BeanFactory` with infrastructure services layered on top.

The initialization row is the one that matters most in practice. The lazy vs eager row explains why `ApplicationContext` is safer for production: misconfigurations fail at startup, not on the first request.

sections.title: When You Actually Touch BeanFactory Directly — and Why It's Rare
sections.content:
In modern Spring Boot applications, you **never instantiate `BeanFactory` yourself**. `SpringApplication.run()` creates an `AnnotationConfigApplicationContext` (or its reactive variant) which implements both `ApplicationContext` and `BeanFactory`. The factory is always there — you just access it through the higher-level context.

The situations where `BeanFactory` matters directly are **framework extension points**. When writing a `BeanFactoryPostProcessor`, you receive the raw `BeanFactory` to modify bean definitions before any beans are created. `PropertySourcesPlaceholderConfigurer` — the processor that resolves `${property}` placeholders — is a `BeanFactoryPostProcessor` that works at this level.

Similarly, `BeanPostProcessor` implementations receive the `BeanFactory` through `BeanFactoryAware` when they need to look up other beans during post-processing. `AutowiredAnnotationBeanPostProcessor` uses this to resolve `@Autowired` dependencies.

The interview takeaway is simple: **use `ApplicationContext` everywhere** unless you're writing a Spring extension. `BeanFactory` is the contract that makes the container work, but application code should never depend on it directly.

A nuance worth mentioning: `ConfigurableApplicationContext` (which `AnnotationConfigApplicationContext` implements) adds `refresh()` and `close()` methods. `SpringApplication.run()` calls `refresh()` to trigger the full bean creation process and registers a JVM shutdown hook that calls `close()`. When writing tests that create `ApplicationContext` manually, always close it in a `finally` block or use `@SpringBootTest` which handles lifecycle automatically — leaked contexts hold database connections open and cause port conflicts in test suites.

sections.title: What ApplicationContext Provides That BeanFactory Cannot — The Infrastructure Layer Spring Boot Depends On
sections.content:
The gap between `BeanFactory` and `ApplicationContext` is not academic. The features that `ApplicationContext` adds are the ones Spring Boot's autoconfiguration, Actuator, and test infrastructure rely on.

**`BeanPostProcessor` detection:** `ApplicationContext` automatically detects and registers beans that implement `BeanPostProcessor` — the mechanism that enables `@Autowired`, `@Transactional`, `@Cacheable`, and `@Async`. With plain `BeanFactory`, you must manually register each post-processor. In practice, this means none of Spring's annotation-based features work with a raw `BeanFactory`.

**`MessageSource` for i18n:** `ApplicationContext` provides message bundle resolution for internationalization. Call `context.getMessage("user.notfound", new Object[]{id}, Locale.ENGLISH)` to resolve locale-specific messages from `messages.properties`. `BeanFactory` has no concept of message sources.

**`ApplicationEvent` publishing:** `ApplicationContext` is an `ApplicationEventPublisher`. Beans can publish events (`context.publishEvent(new UserRegisteredEvent(this, user))`) and listen with `@EventListener`. This is the infrastructure behind Spring Boot's startup events (`ApplicationStartingEvent`, `ApplicationReadyEvent`) and the mechanism for decoupled component communication. `BeanFactory` cannot publish or receive events.

**Resource loading:** `ApplicationContext` extends `ResourceLoader`, enabling classpath, file system, and URL resource loading with a unified API. `ClassPathXmlApplicationContext`, `FileSystemXmlApplicationContext`, and `AnnotationConfigApplicationContext` are all `ApplicationContext` implementations optimized for different configuration sources. None of this is available in `BeanFactory`.

The **eager singleton initialization** difference has a production implication that deserves emphasis. With `BeanFactory`, configuration errors — a missing required property, an unsatisfied `@Autowired` dependency, a `@PostConstruct` method that throws — surface only when the affected bean is first accessed. This means you could deploy a broken application, have it start successfully, and only discover the problem when the first user triggers the broken code path. `ApplicationContext` forces all singleton beans to initialize at startup, converting runtime failures into startup failures. In Kubernetes, this means the pod fails its readiness probe and never receives traffic — the deployment fails cleanly instead of serving errors to users.

sections.title: Key Points
sections.content:
- **`BeanFactory` initializes beans lazily; `ApplicationContext` initializes singletons eagerly** — eager initialization catches configuration errors at startup instead of on the first request in production.
- **`ApplicationContext` auto-detects `BeanPostProcessor` beans** — with plain `BeanFactory`, you must manually register each BPP; without auto-detection, `@Autowired`, `@Transactional`, and all annotation-driven features stop working.
- **You never instantiate `BeanFactory` directly in modern Spring** — `SpringApplication.run()` creates `AnnotationConfigApplicationContext` which implements both; `BeanFactory` is the contract, `ApplicationContext` is what you use.
- **`ApplicationContext` is a superset** — it implements `MessageSource` (i18n), `ApplicationEventPublisher` (events), and `ResourceLoader` on top of `BeanFactory`.
- **`ConfigurableApplicationContext.refresh()` starts the container; `close()` shuts it down** — `SpringApplication` calls `refresh()` automatically and registers a JVM shutdown hook for `close()`.

sections.content:
`BeanFactory` is Spring's root IoC interface — the contract that every container must implement. `ApplicationContext` extends it and adds everything a production application needs. In practice you never use `BeanFactory` directly.

**The key difference: initialization strategy**
- `BeanFactory` initializes beans lazily — created only when first requested via `getBean()`
- `ApplicationContext` creates all singleton beans eagerly at startup — configuration errors, missing dependencies, and broken `@PostConstruct` methods fail immediately instead of on the first user request
- In Kubernetes: eager initialization means a broken pod fails its readiness probe and never receives traffic; lazy initialization means the pod starts successfully and serves errors on the first request

**What `ApplicationContext` adds over `BeanFactory`**
- Auto-detection and registration of `BeanPostProcessor` beans — without this, `@Autowired`, `@Transactional`, `@Async`, and every annotation-driven feature stops working
- `ApplicationEventPublisher` — the infrastructure for Spring's event system and Spring Boot's startup events
- `MessageSource` — internationalization and message bundle resolution
- `ResourceLoader` — unified classpath, file system, and URL resource loading

**When you touch `BeanFactory` directly**
- Writing `BeanFactoryPostProcessor` implementations that modify bean definitions before beans are created
- Writing `BeanPostProcessor` implementations that use `BeanFactoryAware` to look up other beans during post-processing

Application code should always depend on `ApplicationContext`. `BeanFactory` is the framework-extension API.

questions.question: How does Spring AOP work? Explain proxies, JDK dynamic proxies, and CGLIB.
questions.title: How Spring AOP Works (Proxy, JDK vs CGLIB)
questions.direct_answer: Spring AOP creates proxies that wrap target beans and intercept method calls to apply cross-cutting concerns like transactions or caching. It uses JDK dynamic proxies when the bean implements at least one interface, and CGLIB subclass proxies when no interface is present. The proxy is transparent to callers but means that self-invocation (calling a method via 'this') bypasses the proxy and skips advice.

interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Distinguish Spring AOP (proxy-based, method-level only) from AspectJ (full compile/load-time weaving, field-level join points) and explain when you would reach for AspectJ.

sections.title: Why @Transactional Breaks on Self-Invocation — The Proxy Model Explained
sections.content:
The single most common AOP debugging question in Spring interviews is: 'I annotated my method with `@Transactional` but it doesn't work when called from within the same class.' Understanding why requires knowing that **Spring AOP is proxy-based**, not bytecode-based.

When Spring detects an aspect — `@Transactional`, `@Cacheable`, `@Async`, or a custom `@Around` advice — it wraps the target bean in a **proxy object** during the `BeanPostProcessor` phase. Every external call to that bean goes through the proxy, which applies the aspect logic (begin transaction, check cache, run on async thread). But a call from `this.method()` inside the same class bypasses the proxy entirely — it hits the original object directly.

Spring offers two proxy implementations. **JDK dynamic proxies** work when the bean implements an interface — the proxy implements the same interface and delegates to the original. **CGLIB proxies** create a subclass of the concrete class at runtime, which is why Spring Boot defaults to CGLIB (most beans don't implement interfaces). Both intercept external calls identically; neither intercepts internal `this` calls.

This proxy model is simpler and lighter than AspectJ's full compile-time or load-time weaving — but it comes with that self-invocation limitation. Knowing this trade-off and its workarounds is what interviewers test.

sections.title: How Spring Creates Proxies: The BeanPostProcessor That Replaces Your Bean
sections.content:
Proxy creation happens during the `postProcessAfterInitialization` phase of the bean lifecycle. `AbstractAutoProxyCreator` — a `BeanPostProcessor` — scans each bean for applicable advisors (aspects). If any advisor matches (e.g., a `@Transactional` method exists), the post-processor creates a proxy and **returns it instead of the original bean**.

The proxy selection follows a clear rule. If the bean's class implements at least one interface, Spring can use a **JDK dynamic proxy** — it creates a class that implements the same interface and delegates each call through an `InvocationHandler`. If the bean doesn't implement any interface, Spring falls back to **CGLIB**, which generates a subclass at runtime using bytecode generation.

Spring Boot 2.0+ defaults to CGLIB proxies even when interfaces are available, controlled by `spring.aop.proxy-target-class=true`. The reason is practical: JDK proxies require you to inject the interface type, not the concrete class. Code that injects `MyServiceImpl` instead of `MyService` breaks with JDK proxies but works fine with CGLIB. Defaulting to CGLIB eliminates this class of startup errors.

sections.title: The Self-Invocation Trap: Why this.method() Bypasses Every Aspect
Key Points
sections.content:
- **Spring AOP is proxy-based, not bytecode weaving** — Spring wraps the bean in a JDK dynamic proxy or CGLIB subclass; AOP only intercepts public method calls that arrive through the proxy.
- **Self-invocation bypasses the proxy** — `this.method()` refers to the original object, not the proxy; `@Transactional`, `@Async`, and custom aspects are all bypassed on internal calls — the most common AOP debugging scenario.
- **JDK proxy requires interface; CGLIB uses class subclassing** — Spring Boot defaults to CGLIB (`spring.aop.proxy-target-class=true`) because most beans do not implement interfaces and JDK proxies fail when the concrete class is injected.
- **Proxy creation happens in `postProcessAfterInitialization`** — `AbstractAutoProxyCreator` scans each bean for applicable advisors and returns a proxy instead of the original if any match.
- **AspectJ weaving is the escape hatch for self-invocation** — compile-time or load-time AspectJ modifies bytecode directly; it intercepts any method including private ones and internal calls; use it only when proxy limitations are a real constraint.

sections.title: How to Answer This Verbally
sections.content:
Spring AOP is proxy-based — not bytecode weaving. When you annotate a method with `@Transactional` or `@Cacheable`, Spring does not modify your code; it wraps your bean in a proxy object that intercepts external method calls and applies the aspect before or after delegating to the original.

**How the proxy is created**
- During `postProcessAfterInitialization`, `AbstractAutoProxyCreator` scans each bean for applicable advisors
- If any advisor matches, it returns a proxy instead of the original bean — what gets registered in the container is the proxy
- JDK dynamic proxy: requires the bean to implement an interface; Spring Boot defaults to CGLIB even when interfaces exist
- CGLIB proxy: generates a runtime subclass of the concrete class; can proxy any public method

**The self-invocation trap**
- `this.method()` refers to the original object, not the proxy — the aspect never fires
- This is the root cause of every my `@Transactional` is not working bug where one method calls another transactional method on the same class
- Fix: move the called method to a separate bean so the call crosses the proxy boundary, or inject the bean into itself

**Spring AOP vs AspectJ**
- Spring AOP: proxy-based, public methods only, no self-invocation, zero configuration overhead
- AspectJ: bytecode weaving, any method including private ones, self-invocation works — use only when the proxy limitations are a real constraint

questions.question: How do you write pointcut expressions in Spring AOP?

sections.title: The Pattern Language That Decides Where Your Aspect Fires
sections.content:
Every aspect needs to know **where to fire** — which methods, in which classes, under which conditions. That's what pointcut expressions define. They're a pattern language specific to Spring AOP that selects join points (method executions) based on class names, method signatures, annotations, or argument types.

Get it wrong, and your aspect either fires on every method in the application (destroying performance), misses the methods it should target (appearing broken), or — worst case — matches methods in third-party libraries and causes baffling side effects.

Spring AOP supports several pointcut designators, but three dominate production use: **`execution()`** matches by method signature pattern, **`@annotation()`** matches by the presence of an annotation, and **`within()`** matches by declaring class. The rest — `args()`, `target()`, `this()`, `@within()`, `@args()` — are niche tools for advanced scenarios.

The most important thing to understand is that Spring AOP pointcuts only match **Spring-managed bean methods**. A pointcut expression that would match a method on a non-bean object does nothing — Spring AOP works through proxies, and non-beans don't get proxied. Beyond that, Spring AOP only intercepts **public methods** by default when using JDK dynamic proxies. CGLIB proxies can intercept protected and package-private methods, but private methods are always excluded.

A well-designed pointcut is **narrow and intentional**. `execution(* *.*(..))` matches everything — every method on every bean. This causes performance issues and unexpected behavior. Prefer annotation-based pointcuts (`@annotation(Timed)`) for explicitly opt-in behavior, or tightly scoped `execution()` patterns for convention-based behavior.

sections.title: The execution() Expression: Anatomy and Common Patterns
Annotation-Based Pointcuts and Combining Expressions
Key Points
sections.content:
- **`execution()` pattern: `modifiers? return-type declaring-type?.method-name(params)`** — `*` matches one segment; `..` matches zero-or-more sub-packages in a type or zero-or-more parameters in args.
- **`@annotation()` is the safest approach for custom aspects** — explicitly opt-in; only methods carrying the annotation are matched; cannot accidentally match unrelated code.
- **Spring AOP only matches public methods on Spring-managed beans** — non-bean objects are never proxied; protected and private methods are invisible to the proxy.
- **Too-broad `execution(* *.*(..))` proxies everything** — causes measurable performance overhead on every bean and every method call; scope tightly or use `@annotation()` for precision.
- **Named `@Pointcut` methods for reuse** — extract expressions into `@Pointcut`-annotated void methods; reference by name in advice; update one place when package structure changes.

sections.title: How to Answer This Verbally
sections.content:
Pointcut expressions are the pattern language that tells Spring AOP which methods to intercept. Get the pattern wrong and your aspect either misses everything or fires on every method in the application.

**`execution()` — match by method signature**
- Pattern: `execution(modifiers? return-type declaring-type?.method-name(params))`
- `*` matches one path segment; `..` matches zero-or-more sub-packages in a type pattern and any number of parameters in an arg list
- Example: `execution(* com.example.service..*.*(..))` matches all methods on all classes in `service` and any sub-package

**`@annotation()` — match by annotation presence**
- `@Around("@annotation(com.example.Timed)")` — only methods explicitly annotated are intercepted
- The safest approach for custom aspects — explicitly opt-in, no accidental matches on unrelated code
- Lowercase name in the designator binds the annotation instance to a parameter: `@annotation(timed)` gives you access to `timed.value()` in the advice method

**Combining expressions**
- Use `&&`, `||`, `!` to compose: `serviceLayer() && !transactional()` — service methods that are NOT `@Transactional`
- Extract reusable patterns into named `@Pointcut` void methods — update once when the package structure changes

Spring AOP intercepts public methods on Spring-managed beans only. Non-bean objects are never proxied. Private methods are always excluded.

questions.question: What are the @Transactional propagation types and when would you use each?
questions.title: @Transactional — Propagation Types
questions.direct_answer: @Transactional propagation controls how a method behaves when a transaction already exists. REQUIRED (the default) joins an existing transaction or creates one. REQUIRES_NEW always suspends any existing transaction and creates an independent one. MANDATORY, NEVER, NOT_SUPPORTED, SUPPORTS, and NESTED cover more specialized scenarios.

interviewer_intent.testing: Ability to reason about transaction boundaries and choose the right propagation for audit logs, batch jobs, or compensating transactions.
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Using REQUIRED everywhere without understanding that an exception in a nested REQUIRED call will roll back the entire outer transaction.
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Explain NESTED (uses a savepoint so the inner work can be rolled back independently while the outer transaction commits) and contrast it with REQUIRES_NEW (fully separate transaction, separate connection).

sections.content:
Propagation defines how the transactional context is shared between caller and callee. Getting this wrong is a common source of data-consistency bugs — either over-sharing a transaction so an unrelated failure causes a global rollback, or creating too many independent transactions and losing atomicity.

`@Transactional` propagation types control what happens when a transactional method calls another transactional method. The seven propagation levels handle three key scenarios: whether to join an existing transaction, create a new one, or refuse to participate.

**REQUIRED** (default) — join the existing transaction if one exists; otherwise create a new one. This is correct for most service methods. If the inner method throws, the entire transaction rolls back because both methods share the same physical transaction.

**REQUIRES_NEW** — always create a new physical transaction, suspending the outer one. The inner transaction commits or rolls back independently. Use it for operations that must succeed regardless of the outer transaction's outcome — audit logging, notification sending, or idempotency token recording.

**NESTED** — create a savepoint within the existing transaction. If the inner method fails, only the work since the savepoint is rolled back; the outer transaction can catch the exception and continue. This requires JDBC savepoint support and is not supported by all JPA providers.

**SUPPORTS** — run in the existing transaction if one exists; otherwise run non-transactionally. Useful for read methods that benefit from transaction consistency when called from a transactional context but work fine without one.

**MANDATORY** — requires an existing transaction; throws `IllegalTransactionStateException` if none exists. Use it to enforce that a method is never called standalone — it must always be part of a larger unit of work.

**NOT_SUPPORTED** — suspend any existing transaction and run non-transactionally. Useful for operations like cache warmup or external API calls that should not participate in the caller's transaction.

**NEVER** — throw an exception if a transaction exists. The inverse of MANDATORY — enforces that the method is never called within a transaction context.
sections.title: Why REQUIRED Is the Default — and Why It Causes the Most Subtle Bugs
All Seven Propagation Types — Decision at a Glance
sections.content:
The seven propagation types answer one question: **what should happen to the transaction context when this method is called?** The answer depends on whether the operation should share the caller's unit-of-work, needs isolation from it, or must enforce a specific transactional context.

| Propagation | Existing Tx? | Behavior | Classic Use Case |
|---|---|---|---|
| `REQUIRED` (default) | Yes | Join it | Service layer methods |
| `REQUIRED` | No | Create new | Service layer methods |
| `REQUIRES_NEW` | Yes | Suspend + create new | Audit logging, notifications |
| `REQUIRES_NEW` | No | Create new | Audit logging, notifications |
| `NESTED` | Yes | Savepoint + continue | Optional sub-operations in batch |
| `NESTED` | No | Create new | Optional sub-operations |
| `SUPPORTS` | Yes | Join it | Read-only reporting queries |
| `SUPPORTS` | No | Run non-transactionally | Read-only reporting queries |
| `NOT_SUPPORTED` | Yes | Suspend + run non-tx | Legacy code, long-running reports |
| `MANDATORY` | Yes | Join it | Internal methods always called within tx |
| `MANDATORY` | No | Throw exception | Internal methods always called within tx |
| `NEVER` | Yes | Throw exception | Batch exports that must not hold locks |
| `NEVER` | No | Run non-transactionally | Batch exports |

The most important distinction in practice: **REQUIRED rolls back together.** If an inner `REQUIRED` method throws, the entire outer transaction rolls back. Developers who add an audit log call inside a business transaction and use `REQUIRED` find their audit log disappears whenever the business transaction fails — because the exception propagates and the entire unit of work (including the audit insert) rolls back. The fix is `REQUIRES_NEW`.

sections.title: REQUIRES_NEW vs NESTED — The Two Isolation Mechanisms and When Each Fails
Key Points
sections.content:
- **`REQUIRED` rolls back together** — an exception in an inner `REQUIRED` call rolls back the entire outer transaction; an audit log inside a `REQUIRED` call disappears if the business transaction fails.
- **`REQUIRES_NEW` uses a separate physical connection** — suspends the outer transaction and borrows a new connection from the pool; the inner commit is permanent even if the outer transaction later rolls back; doubles connection usage under load.
- **`NESTED` uses a savepoint on the same connection** — inner failure rolls back to the savepoint; outer can catch and continue; outer failure rolls back everything including the nested work.
- **Self-invocation bypasses `@Transactional` entirely** — regardless of propagation type, calling a `@Transactional` method via `this` goes through the original object, not the proxy; no transaction management.
- **`REQUIRES_NEW` connection exhaustion at scale** — each `REQUIRES_NEW` call borrows a connection while the outer still holds one; in a high-throughput service with multiple audit calls per request, connection pool exhaustion becomes the failure mode.

sections.title: How to Answer This Verbally
sections.content:
`@Transactional` propagation controls what happens to the transaction context when one transactional method calls another. Getting it wrong produces data-consistency bugs — audit logs that vanish, operations that should be independent sharing a rollback boundary.

**`REQUIRED` (the default)**
- Joins the existing transaction if one is active; creates a new one if not
- Inner and outer method share the same physical transaction — an exception anywhere rolls back everything
- The audit log trap: write an audit log inside a `REQUIRED` call and the outer transaction fails — the audit log disappears with it

**`REQUIRES_NEW`**
- Always creates a new, independent transaction, suspending the outer one
- Uses a separate database connection — the inner commit is permanent even if the outer transaction later rolls back
- The right choice for audit logging and notifications that must persist regardless of the business outcome
- The cost: two open connections simultaneously; under high load with many `REQUIRES_NEW` calls per request, connection pool exhaustion becomes the failure mode

**`NESTED`**
- Creates a savepoint within the same physical connection
- Inner failure rolls back to the savepoint; the outer transaction can catch the exception and continue
- Outer failure rolls back everything — all work on the same connection
- Lower resource cost than `REQUIRES_NEW` but requires JDBC savepoint support

Regardless of propagation type: calling a `@Transactional` method via `this` bypasses the proxy — no transaction management at all. The propagation setting has no effect on self-invocation.

questions.title: Spring Events (@EventListener, ApplicationEventPublisher)

sections.title: Why Spring Events Are Synchronous by Default — and Why That Catches Everyone
sections.content:
The biggest misconception about Spring Events is that they're asynchronous. They're not. By default, when you call `applicationEventPublisher.publishEvent(event)`, every `@EventListener` for that event type runs **synchronously on the same thread**, in the same transaction. A slow listener blocks the publisher. An exception in a listener kills the publisher's flow.

This matters because developers reach for events to 'decouple' components — send an email after an order is placed, update a cache after a record changes. But synchronous events don't decouple execution — they only decouple the **compile-time dependency**. The publisher doesn't import the listener class, but they still share the same thread and transaction at runtime.

True decoupling requires either **`@Async` on the listener** (separate thread pool) or **`@TransactionalEventListener`** (fires after the transaction commits/rolls back). Understanding this distinction — compile-time decoupling vs runtime decoupling — is what separates a surface-level answer from a production-aware one.

Key Points

Spring's event system implements the Observer pattern within the container. A service publishes an event; listeners react without any direct compile-time coupling. But the most important thing to understand is what decoupling does and does not mean here.

**Events are synchronous by default**

**`@TransactionalEventListener` — for post-commit actions**
- The production pattern for notifications, emails, and cache updates that must only happen after a successful commit

- Add `@Async` to the listener method — runs on a separate thread pool, fully decoupling execution timing
- Requires `@EnableAsync` and a custom `TaskExecutor`; without it, `SimpleAsyncTaskExecutor` creates unbounded threads

questions.question: What is @Conditional in Spring and how do you implement a custom condition?
questions.title: @Conditional and Custom Conditions
questions.direct_answer: @Conditional tells the container to register a bean only when a given Condition implementation returns true. Spring Boot's auto-configuration is built almost entirely on @Conditional variants like @ConditionalOnClass, @ConditionalOnMissingBean, and @ConditionalOnProperty.

interviewer_intent.testing: Understanding of Spring's conditional bean registration model, which is the foundation of Spring Boot auto-configuration.
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Not knowing the difference between @Profile (environment-based) and @Conditional (arbitrary logic), or not realizing that @ConditionalOnMissingBean is how Spring Boot lets you override auto-configured beans.
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Explain the Condition interface's ConditionContext, show how to write a condition that checks an environment property, and describe the ordering issue: conditions are evaluated during the BeanDefinitionRegistry phase, before any beans are created.

sections.title: Why @Conditional Is the Engine Behind Every Spring Boot Auto-Configuration
sections.content:
Every time Spring Boot 'magically' configures a `DataSource` because H2 is on the classpath, or sets up a `JdbcTemplate` because `spring-boot-starter-jdbc` is present, the mechanism is `@Conditional`. Spring Boot's auto-configuration classes are annotated with **`@ConditionalOnClass`**, **`@ConditionalOnMissingBean`**, **`@ConditionalOnProperty`** — all of which are specialized forms of `@Conditional`.

The core interface is simple: `Condition` has a single method, `matches(ConditionContext, AnnotatedTypeMetadata)`, that returns `true` or `false`. If `true`, the annotated `@Bean` or `@Configuration` class is registered. If `false`, Spring skips it entirely — no bean definition, no instantiation, no error.

This is fundamentally different from `@Profile`, which is just `@Conditional` with a built-in condition that checks `spring.profiles.active`. Custom `@Conditional` can check anything: classpath contents, system properties, environment variables, database availability, feature flags from a remote service. The evaluation happens at **bean definition time** — before any bean is instantiated — making it the earliest decision point in the Spring lifecycle.

sections.title: Building a Custom Condition: Feature Flags Without External Libraries
How Spring Boot's @ConditionalOnMissingBean Enables Override-Friendly Defaults
sections.content:
The most important built-in condition is **`@ConditionalOnMissingBean`** — it registers a bean only if no bean of that type already exists. This is the mechanism that makes Spring Boot auto-configuration override-friendly.

When Spring Boot auto-configures a `DataSource`, the `@Bean` method is annotated with `@ConditionalOnMissingBean(DataSource.class)`. If you define your own `DataSource` bean in a `@Configuration` class, your bean is registered first (user configurations are processed before auto-configurations), and the auto-configured one is silently skipped.

This **convention-over-configuration** model works because of evaluation order. User-defined `@Configuration` classes are always processed before `AutoConfiguration` classes (which live in `META-INF/spring/org.springframework.boot.autoconfigure.AutoConfiguration.imports`). By the time auto-configuration runs, your custom beans are already in the registry, and `@ConditionalOnMissingBean` detects them.

Other useful built-in conditions include `@ConditionalOnClass` (checks if a class is on the classpath — how Spring Boot knows to configure JPA only when Hibernate is present), `@ConditionalOnProperty` (checks a property value), and `@ConditionalOnWebApplication` (only in servlet or reactive web contexts). Together, these conditions form the **decision tree** that makes Spring Boot applications auto-configure correctly without manual setup.

sections.title: Key Points
sections.content:
- **`@Conditional` is the engine behind every Spring Boot auto-configuration** — `@ConditionalOnClass`, `@ConditionalOnMissingBean`, `@ConditionalOnProperty` are all specialized `@Conditional` annotations.
- **Conditions are evaluated at bean definition time** — before any bean is created; a condition checking for the existence of another bean uses the `BeanDefinitionRegistry`, not the live container.
- **`@ConditionalOnMissingBean` makes auto-config override-friendly** — user-defined beans are registered before auto-configurations; the condition finds your bean already in the registry and skips the auto-configured one.
- **`@Profile` is just `@Conditional` with a built-in condition** — it checks `spring.profiles.active`; any logic you would put in a custom `Condition.matches()` can also drive bean registration.
- **Never call `context.getBean()` inside `Condition.matches()`** — beans may not be created yet at evaluation time; use the `BeanDefinitionRegistry` to check if a bean definition exists.

sections.content:
Every time Spring Boot automatically sets up a `DataSource` because H2 is on the classpath, or skips configuring `JdbcTemplate` because you already defined one, the mechanism is `@Conditional`. It is the decision engine behind all of Spring Boot's auto-configuration.

**The core interface**
- `Condition` has one method: `matches(ConditionContext, AnnotatedTypeMetadata)` returns `true` or `false`
- If `false`, Spring skips the annotated `@Bean` or `@Configuration` entirely — no bean definition, no instantiation, no error
- Evaluation happens at bean definition time, before any bean is created — not at runtime

**The built-in conditions**
- `@ConditionalOnClass` — checks if a class is on the classpath; how Spring Boot knows to configure JPA only when Hibernate is present
- `@ConditionalOnMissingBean` — registers a bean only if no bean of that type already exists; user configurations are processed before auto-configurations, so your custom bean wins
- `@ConditionalOnProperty` — evaluates a property value at startup

**Custom conditions**
- Implement `Condition`, use `ConditionContext` to check the `Environment`, `ClassLoader`, `BeanDefinitionRegistry`, or `ResourceLoader`
- Compose into a custom annotation: `@ConditionalOnFeature("dark-mode")` backed by a condition that reads `feature.dark-mode.enabled`

`@Profile` is just `@Conditional` with a built-in condition that checks active profiles. Anything you want to conditionally enable — a feature flag, an environment-specific service, a paid-tier bean graph — can be driven by a custom `@Conditional`.

questions.question: How do Spring profiles work? Explain @Profile and spring.profiles.active.
questions.title: Spring Profiles (@Profile, spring.profiles.active)
questions.direct_answer: Spring profiles allow you to register beans conditionally based on the active environment. A bean annotated with @Profile("prod") is only created when the 'prod' profile is active. Profiles are activated via spring.profiles.active in application.properties, an environment variable, a JVM argument, or programmatically.

interviewer_intent.testing: Practical ability to configure environment-specific beans (datasources, mocks, feature flags) and understanding of profile inheritance.
interviewer_intent.common_mistake: Hardcoding environment-specific values in beans instead of using profiles, or not knowing that multiple profiles can be active simultaneously.
interviewer_intent.to_stand_out: Explain profile groups (spring.profiles.group.production=prod,monitoring) introduced in Spring Boot 2.4, and the difference between default profile and fallback profile behavior.

sections.content:
Profiles provide a first-class mechanism for separating environment-specific configuration. Rather than using if/else logic or property placeholders throughout your beans, you declare entire bean graphs that are only wired in specific environments. Spring Boot extends this to application.properties files (application-prod.properties) and profile groups.

Spring Profiles provide a mechanism to conditionally register beans and load configuration based on the active environment — development, staging, production, test. They are one of the core building blocks for environment-specific behavior in Spring Boot applications.

**Defining profile-specific beans:** Annotate a `@Configuration` class or individual `@Bean` method with `@Profile("dev")`. The bean is only registered when the `dev` profile is active. You can use negation (`@Profile("!prod")`) to register a bean in all profiles except production.

**Activating profiles:** Set `spring.profiles.active=dev,local` in `application.properties`, as an environment variable (`SPRING_PROFILES_ACTIVE`), a JVM argument (`-Dspring.profiles.active=dev`), or programmatically via `SpringApplication.setAdditionalProfiles()`. Multiple profiles can be active simultaneously.

**Profile-specific property files:** Spring Boot loads `application-{profile}.yml` (or `.properties`) for each active profile. Properties in profile-specific files override those in `application.yml`. This is the primary mechanism for environment-specific configuration: database URLs, logging levels, feature flags.

**Profile groups (Spring Boot 2.4+):** `spring.profiles.group.production=proddb,prodmq` defines a group so activating `production` automatically activates `proddb` and `prodmq`. This reduces the number of profiles you need to explicitly list.

**Testing:** `@ActiveProfiles("test")` on integration test classes activates the `test` profile, loading `application-test.yml` with in-memory databases, mock service URLs, and debug logging. This isolation ensures tests never accidentally hit production resources.
sections.title: Why Profiles Exist: Environment-Specific Configuration Without Code Changes
Define Profile-Specific Beans
sections.description: Annotate beans or @Configuration classes with @Profile. The bean is registered only when the named profile is active. You can negate a profile with '!' or use logical expressions.

sections.title: Activate Profiles
sections.description: Profiles can be activated through multiple mechanisms. Multiple profiles can be active simultaneously.
sections.content:
Spring profiles can be activated through multiple mechanisms, and they follow a **priority order** that matters when the same property is set in different places. The highest-priority source wins.

**Command-line arguments** have the highest priority. `--spring.profiles.active=prod` overrides everything else. This is the standard for containerized deployments where the orchestrator (Kubernetes, ECS) passes environment configuration at launch.

**Environment variables** are next: `SPRING_PROFILES_ACTIVE=prod`. This is the Docker-friendly approach — you set it in the Dockerfile or the container spec.

**`application.properties`** is the lowest priority: `spring.profiles.active=dev`. This is typically the developer default — local development runs with `dev` unless overridden.

```properties
# application.properties — developer default
spring.profiles.active=dev

# Override via command line:
# java -jar app.jar --spring.profiles.active=prod

# Override via environment variable (Docker/K8s):
# SPRING_PROFILES_ACTIVE=prod
```

Multiple profiles can be active simultaneously — `spring.profiles.active=prod,monitoring` activates both. Beans annotated with either `@Profile("prod")` or `@Profile("monitoring")` will be registered.

sections.title: Profile-Specific Property Files
sections.description: Spring Boot loads application-{profile}.properties (or .yml) automatically when a profile is active. Profile-specific properties override the base application.properties.
sections.code:
# application.properties (base)
app.name=InterviewExplainer
logging.level.root=INFO

# application-prod.properties (loaded when prod is active)
spring.datasource.url=jdbc:postgresql://prod-db:5432/app
logging.level.root=WARN

# application-dev.properties (loaded when dev is active)
spring.datasource.url=jdbc:h2:mem:devdb
logging.level.com.app=DEBUG
sections.content:
Beyond beans, profiles control which **property files** Spring loads. The naming convention is `application-{profile}.properties` (or `.yml`). When the `prod` profile is active, Spring loads both `application.properties` (base) and `application-prod.properties` (override). Profile-specific properties **take precedence** over base properties.

This is how you vary configuration like database URLs, logging levels, and feature flags without touching code. The base file defines defaults; the profile file overrides what's different.

```properties
# application.properties (base — always loaded)
app.cache.ttl=60s
logging.level.root=INFO

# application-dev.properties (loaded when 'dev' profile active)
logging.level.root=DEBUG
spring.jpa.show-sql=true

# application-prod.properties (loaded when 'prod' profile active)
app.cache.ttl=3600s
logging.level.root=WARN
```

A common mistake is putting production secrets directly in `application-prod.properties` and committing them to version control. Profile-specific files should contain non-sensitive overrides. Secrets belong in environment variables, Vault, or AWS Secrets Manager — injected at runtime, never stored in the repository.

sections.title: Profile Groups (Spring Boot 2.4+)
sections.description: Profile groups let you activate multiple fine-grained profiles with a single name. This avoids long comma-separated profile lists in deployment scripts.
sections.code:
# application.properties
# Activating 'production' activates prod + monitoring + security-hardened
spring.profiles.group.production=prod,monitoring,security-hardened

# Activating 'local' activates dev + mockservices
spring.profiles.group.local=dev,mockservices

# Then in deployment:
spring.profiles.active=production
sections.content:
Spring Boot 2.4 introduced **profile groups**, which solve the problem of activating multiple related profiles together. Before groups, deploying to production meant setting `spring.profiles.active=prod,monitoring,security` — a list that grows with every new concern and is easy to get wrong.

With groups, you define composite profiles in `application.properties` and activate just the group name.

```properties
# Define groups — activating 'production' activates all three
spring.profiles.group.production=prod,monitoring,security
spring.profiles.group.development=dev,local-cache,debug-logging

# Now just activate the group
spring.profiles.active=production
# Equivalent to: spring.profiles.active=prod,monitoring,security
```

Groups keep environment configuration **manageable as the number of concerns grows**. Instead of every deployment script knowing which individual profiles to activate, it activates a single semantic group. Adding a new monitoring profile means editing the group definition in one place, not updating every deployment pipeline.

sections.title: Key Points
sections.content:
- **`@Profile("!prod")` registers in all profiles except production** — negation syntax enables beans that exist in every environment except one; common for debug tooling and test data seeders.
- **Multiple profiles can be active simultaneously** — `spring.profiles.active=prod,monitoring` activates both; beans annotated with either profile are registered.
- **Profile-specific property files override the base** — `application-prod.properties` overrides `application.properties` for any key present in both; the base file provides defaults.
- **Profile groups (Spring Boot 2.4+)** — `spring.profiles.group.production=prod,monitoring,security` lets you activate a composite with a single name; keeps deployment scripts from growing long profile lists.
- **Activation priority: command-line > env var > `application.properties`** — `--spring.profiles.active=prod` on the command line overrides `SPRING_PROFILES_ACTIVE` env var, which overrides the property file.
- **`@ActiveProfiles("test")` in tests** — activates the `test` profile for `@SpringBootTest`, loading `application-test.properties` with H2, mock service URLs, and debug logging.

sections.title: How to Answer This Verbally
sections.content:
Spring profiles let you register different bean graphs and load different property files based on the active environment — without changing code or rebuilding the artifact. The same JAR behaves differently in dev, staging, and production based on which profiles are active.

**Profile-specific beans**
- `@Profile("prod")` on a `@Bean` or `@Configuration` class — only registered when `prod` is active
- `@Profile("!prod")` — registered in every profile except production; common for debug tooling and mock services
- Multiple active profiles at once: `spring.profiles.active=prod,monitoring` — beans from both profiles are registered

**Activating profiles — priority order**
- Command-line `--spring.profiles.active=prod` — highest priority, overrides everything else
- Environment variable `SPRING_PROFILES_ACTIVE=prod` — Docker and Kubernetes standard
- `spring.profiles.active=dev` in `application.properties` — developer default, lowest priority

**Profile-specific property files**
- `application-prod.properties` loads automatically when `prod` is active and overrides the base `application.properties` for any key present in both
- Base file sets defaults; profile files override what is environment-specific

**Profile groups (Spring Boot 2.4+)**
- `spring.profiles.group.production=prod,monitoring,security` — activate `production` and all three sub-profiles activate automatically

In tests, `@ActiveProfiles("test")` loads `application-test.properties` — typically with an H2 in-memory database, mock service URLs, and verbose logging. Tests never accidentally hit production resources.

sections.title: Why SpEL Exists When Property Placeholders Already Work
sections.content:
Property placeholders (`${key}`) do simple lookups — they find a value by name and inject it. But what if you need to **compute** a value? Split a comma-separated string into a list, call a method on another bean, evaluate a conditional expression, or access system properties?

**Spring Expression Language (SpEL)** fills this gap. The `#{expression}` syntax evaluates arbitrary expressions at bean creation time — method calls, arithmetic, ternary operators, collection projections, and references to other beans in the container. It's a mini programming language embedded in annotations.

The practical trade-off is readability. SpEL expressions can do almost anything, but complex expressions in annotations become **opaque and hard to debug**. When a `SpelEvaluationException` fires at startup, the stack trace points to the annotation, not to a line of Java code you can step through. The rule of thumb: use SpEL for simple transformations (splitting strings, defaulting values, referencing beans) and move complex logic to `@PostConstruct` methods where you get proper IDE support and debuggability.

sections.title: The Three SpEL Patterns You'll Actually Use in Production
When SpEL Becomes a Maintenance Problem: The Complexity Threshold
sections.content:
SpEL's power becomes a liability when expressions get complex. An expression like `#{@beanA.method() != null ? @beanA.method().transform(@beanB.config) : 'fallback'}` does work — but it's untestable, undebuggable, and invisible to IDE refactoring tools.

The **complexity threshold** is roughly one level of nesting. A simple `split()`, a bean reference, or a ternary with literal values is fine. Anything that chains method calls, references multiple beans, or includes business logic belongs in a `@PostConstruct` method or a dedicated `@Configuration` class.

Another trap is **security with user input**. SpEL expressions that include user-provided values can be exploited for **Remote Code Execution** — the `T(Runtime).exec()` operator can execute arbitrary system commands. Never construct SpEL expressions from user input. Spring Security's `@PreAuthorize("hasRole('ADMIN')")` is safe because the expression is a compile-time constant, not user-generated.

For `@Value` annotations specifically, SpEL evaluation happens **once at bean creation time**. The value is injected and cached — there's no live re-evaluation if the underlying property changes. For dynamic values that need to change at runtime, use `Environment.getProperty()` directly or Spring Cloud's `@RefreshScope`.

sections.title: SpEL Beyond Configuration: Security Expressions and @Value in Tests
sections.content:
SpEL appears in three contexts beyond `@Value`: Spring Security's method-level authorization, Spring Data's `@Query` annotations, and Spring Cache's condition expressions.

**Spring Security method expressions** like `@PreAuthorize("#orderId == authentication.principal.userId or hasRole('ADMIN')")` use SpEL to evaluate complex authorization logic. The `#orderId` reference binds to the method parameter by name (requires `-parameters` compiler flag or `@P` annotation). `authentication.principal` accesses the authenticated user object. These expressions run on every method invocation and are evaluated by Spring's `MethodSecurityExpressionHandler` — a dedicated SpEL expression evaluator with security-specific root objects.

**Spring Data `@Query`** supports SpEL for dynamic query fragments: `@Query("SELECT e FROM #{#entityName} WHERE e.status = :status")` where `#{#entityName}` resolves to the entity class name at runtime. This enables generic repository queries in base repository classes.

**Cache condition expressions** control when caching applies: `@Cacheable(value = "orders", condition = "#id > 100", unless = "#result == null")`. `condition` prevents caching when the expression is false (evaluated before method execution). `unless` prevents caching when the expression is true (evaluated after, with access to `#result`).

In tests, `@Value("#{T(java.lang.Math).PI}")` injects mathematical constants. `@Value("#{systemProperties['java.home']}")` injects JVM properties. These are test-only patterns — production code should use property sources, not hardcoded values. SpEL in `@ConditionalOnExpression` enables conditional bean creation: `@ConditionalOnExpression("${feature.enabled:false} and '${env}' == 'prod'")` combines property lookup with logical evaluation.

sections.title: Key Points
sections.content:
- **`${}` is property lookup; `#{}` is SpEL expression** — they are different syntaxes; `${}` always resolves first, `#{}` evaluates the result; nesting order is always `${}` inside `#{}`.
- **SpEL is evaluated once at bean creation, not at call time** — the value is injected and cached; live re-evaluation requires `@RefreshScope` or calling `Environment.getProperty()` directly.
- **SpEL plus user input equals Remote Code Execution risk** — `T(Runtime).exec()` can run arbitrary system commands; never construct SpEL expressions from user-provided values.
- **Complex SpEL in annotations is opaque and hard to debug** — `SpelEvaluationException` points to the annotation, not a line of Java; move logic exceeding one level of nesting to `@PostConstruct` or a `@Configuration` method.
- **SpEL powers Spring Security method expressions** — `@PreAuthorize("#orderId == authentication.principal.userId")` evaluates SpEL with security-specific root objects on every protected method call.

sections.title: How to Answer This Verbally
sections.content:
Property placeholders (`${key}`) do simple lookups. Spring Expression Language (`#{}`) evaluates arbitrary expressions — method calls, ternary operators, bean references, arithmetic. The syntax difference matters: `${}` resolves a value by name; `#{}` computes one.

**The `${}` placeholder**
- Resolves against Spring's `Environment` — `application.properties`, environment variables, system properties
- Missing key without a default throws `IllegalArgumentException` at startup
- Colon syntax for defaults: `${key:fallback}` — no space after the colon

**The `#{}` SpEL syntax**
- Evaluates expressions at bean creation time: method calls, ternary operators, bean property access, static method invocation with `T(ClassName)`
- Most common production pattern: `#{'${csv}'.split(',')}` — `${}` resolves the property, SpEL transforms it into a `List`; always `${}` inside `#{}`, never reversed
- If the expression fails at startup: `SpelEvaluationException` pointing to the annotation, not to debuggable code

**Where SpEL appears beyond `@Value`**
- Spring Security: `@PreAuthorize("hasRole('ADMIN') or #userId == authentication.principal.id")` — evaluated with security-specific root objects on every call
- `@Cacheable(condition = "#id > 100", unless = "#result == null")` — `condition` evaluated before execution, `unless` after with access to `#result`

Keep SpEL expressions simple — one transformation, one method call. Anything more complex belongs in a `@PostConstruct` method where you have IDE support, proper error handling, and a debugger.
